speechtext: 50TH ANNIVERSARY OF UNITED NATIONS

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Agreed.\nGovernment Orders']

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of External Relations and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Seniors)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my privilege this morning to remind the House that last Tuesday marked the launching of Canadian activities to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the United Nations. The international community has taken this opportunity to start a world dialogue on how the UN will meet the commitments formulated in the charter during the 21st century.

At lunch last Tbesday I had the opportunity to welcome Ambassador Richard Butler of Australia who is the permanent representative of Australia to the United Nations and chairman of the United Nations preparatory
committee for its 50th anniversary. The members of the Canadian national committee for the United Nations 50th anniversary were also present.
It is a true measure of the importance that we in Canada attach to this organization that such a distinguished group of Canadians, led by its chair, Douglas Roche, has agreed to serve on the committee.

This committee is a Canadian initiative in response to an appeal by the UN Secretary-General, Mr. Boutros-Boutros Ghali. Creating this committee is a first step in a series of events, culminating in the 50th anniversary of the signing of the United Nations charter on October 24, 1995.
Canada has always maintained a clear commitment to the principles of the charter and international co-operation, and our contribution in this respect has won international recognition. Since 1945, this commitment has been the driving force of our foreign policy. With genuine enthusiasm, Canadians are looking forward to celebrating this anniversary.
Many activities will take place in this country, including an international symposium in Quebec City in October 1995 to mark the 50th anniversary of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
In Montreal a special committee has been set up to mark the 50th anniversary of the International Civil Aviation Organization. December 7, 1994, has been designated International Civil Aviation Day and Canada Post will issue a special stamp on that occasion.
These are only a few of the many ways Canadians will celebrate the UN's anniversary in 1995. As a member of the United Nations, Canada has many reasons to celebrate.
Since 1945 our country has contributed in many different ways towards building the UN. It was involved in drafting the charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Canada has often held a seat on the Security Council where its efforts have produced excellent results. Furthermore, thousands of Canadians have

May 27, 1993
Routine Proceedings
worked, and are still working, for the UN and its specialized agencies.

One of Canada's most challenging and visible UN roles is that of the international peacekeeper. We have been actively involved in almost every peacekeeping operation since Lester B. Pearson, Canadian Nobel laureate and former Prime Minister, did so much to develop the concept.

We make a major contribution to UN peacekeeping operations, through the participation of our troops and the efforts of Canadian citizens deployed throughout the world. Canada has taken its moral and financial responsibilities in this respect very seriously.
Finally, I would like to remind the House of the splendid work being done by the United Nations Association in Canada. This organization informs the Canadian public about the UN and is now playing an important role in setting up the national committee for the 50th anniversary.
The charter starts with the words "We the peoples of the United Nations" the theme recommended by the UN for 1995. It is incumbent on us, the people of Canada, to ensure that the 50th anniversary of the United Nations is celebrated in a true spirit of participation, as reflected not only in official ceremonies but above all in a renewed commitment by our country to the principles set forth in the UN charter.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity on behalf of the Official Opposition to comment upon this very important occasion on which we will be honouring the 50th anniversary of the United Nations. We certainly look forward to the various celebrations the minister was talking about.
However the most important way to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the United Nations is not to engage in a series of public relations exercises or anniversary parties at which we have coloured lights, balloons, cakes and
candles but to engage in a fundamental reform of the charter of the United Nations.
There was nothing in the statement by the minister that indicated in any way, shape or form that this government has any plan of action to deal substantially with the reform of the charter of the United Nations to bring it up to date and make it relevant to the kinds of conditions we face in the world today.
Surely, as we look at the tragedy in Bosnia and the complete breakdown, the shameful and embarrassing lack of action by western powers to deal with the murder and genocide in that poor country, we realize just how deeply we need to look at the way in which the world community organizes itself to stop the new kinds of conflicts and the new kinds of transgressions of human rights.
There is an enormous level of poverty emerging in the world. The United Nations has said that if we do not take a new look at the question of jobs, employment and poverty we will be engulfed by a whole new generation of conflicts. We need agencies in the United Nations with the effective and efficient ability to deliver these reforms. Surely, we must look at a fundamental review of the charter.

There is nothing in the minister's statement suggesting a task force on UN reform. Celebrating is fine, but we need a firm statement from the Government of Canada on UN reform.

This week our leader announced the foreign policy platform of our own party and put forward as a central point the need to have a charter review. After 50 years of the United Nations it is time for Canada to take the lead in undertaking a major revision of crucial matters dealing with peace, security, economic organization and the financing of the UN. Yet there is nothing in this statement to indicate that this government has the slightest interest in that fundamental requirement.
To prove the point, we know that by the end of June the United Nations Secretary-General has requested all member states to submit proposals for reform of the Security Council and the composition of the Security Council. This government has not even submitted a proposal. It has not had a debate in the House. It has not
May 27, 1993

had any discussion with the NGOs across Canada on this fundamental question of how to reform the Security Council. It is asleep at the switch at a crucial time in the history of the world.
When the minister speaks about the past accomplishments of Canada in leading the development, evolution and creation of the UN, she speaks in the past tense. We are concerned about the future tense and whether Canada will continue to have a leadership role in providing for fundamental reform and change to make the United Nations a full, complete and effective representation of the world community.
In this document, this statement there is no indication of any of that kind of commitment, preparation, readiness and willingness to take on the reform of the UN as a central thrust of Canadian foreign policy.
There is a wonderful book written by Dean Acheson, the former U.S. Secretary of State, called Present at the Creation. He talks about how he and a generation of statesmen, including many Canadians such as Lester Pearson, Paul Martin and others, plus a very distinguished group of civil servants, took part in developing the fundamental structures of the UN in 1945-46.
We think it is time to be present at the recreation of the United Nations and to mobilize the best brains, talent, integrity and energy of Canadians to once again bring Canadian leadership into the world to make sure the UN is able to fulfil its rightful and only place as a full and effective democratic representative for the new kind of world that we live in and to deal with the emerging problems of human rights, economic development and peace and security.
We think the best way for Canadians to celebrate the 50th anniversary is to make sure that the 100th anniversary of the United Nations will also be celebrated in a world where there is peace, security, justice and equality. The best way to celebrate the UN is to put our best resources to work to rebuild the United Nations.

Madam Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to respond as the spokesperson on external affairs for the New Demo-
Routine Proceedings
cratic Party as well as a member of the Canadian committee for the 50th anniversary of the United Nations.
I want to respond briefly to this statement by the Minister for External Relations. I want to begin my brief response by indicating my concern and disappointment that on this opportunity for the minister to indicate a serious and significant commitment by the Government of Canada to fundamental reform of the United Nations, to a recognition that the United Nations of October 1945 does not reflect the realities and priorities of the world today, we heard a simple affirmation of the fact that the 50th anniversary is coming up and that Canada will be playing a role in it.
We heard nothing whatsoever about the direction this government believes the United Nations should be going in the next decade or more. Neither did we hear about specific proposals with respect to some of the changes in focus and structure of the United Nations..
The members of the external affairs committee met on Tuesday with Ambassador Richard Butler, the permanent representative of Australia to the United Nations who is chairing the United Nations preparatory committee on the 50th anniversary. He indicated that a number of countries are showing leadership. They are playing a major role in looking at issues such as the reform of the Security Council, a revamping of the financial footing of the United Nations and so on.
Where is Canada's voice? Where is Canada's leadership on this or any of the other important issues facing the United Nations as we approach the 50th anniversary?
We know the challenges that face the United Nations today, particularly a fundamental review of the United Nations charter, must be put in the context of a redefinition of security itself. We need a recognition of the principles of common security, that the greatest threats to that security are poverty and global imbalances in wealth and power between north and south and between rich and poor.	.
We have a planet on which 40,000 children die each day of preventable hunger and disease. We have a planet on which international financial institutions, whether the IMF or the World Bank, contribute to the problem

May 27, 1993
Routine Proceedings
instead of contributing to a redistribution of wealth and power to the poor and those in peril.
We know that the threats to the global environment such as global wanning, deforestation, poisoning of the air, water and soil and the threat of nuclear weapons are challenges that a new, invigorated and strengthened United Nations must face. Indeed, we welcome the recent proposal of a number of international NGOs to challenge the legality of nuclear weapons as being illegal before the International Court of Justice.
We know the United Nations must be fundamentally reformed to deal with the tragic reality that war is still all too real on this planet. There are some 40 wars which are still being fought, the most visible and the most tragic of course in the former Yugoslavia with ethnic cleansing still under way.
We had hoped in October 1945, as we emerged from the horrors of the Holocaust and World War II, that we would never again see war. We know however that wish has certainly not been fulfilled.
We should be using the opportunity of the 50th anniversary of the United Nations to examine with care a number of proposals for strengthening the UN.

The United Nations Secretary-General, Mr. Boutros-Ghali, presented a document entitled Agenda for Peace. It contains several excellent ideas which the Government of Canada should consider. Mr. Speaker, what is the Canadian government's position on Agenda for Peace? We still do not know. What is the Canadian government's position on the Stockholm Initiative which puts forward several concrete proposals to improve the status of the United Nations?

Finally, as we look at democratizing the United Nations, at expanding the membership of the Security Council, at putting the UN on a sounder financial footing, strengthening the International Court of Justice, establishing a world criminal court and a United Nations parliamentary assembly, let us recognize that the fundamental commitment too of the United Nations to human rights is at the core of this redefinition. Hopefully the upcoming world conference on human
rights will recognize the importance of establishing a special high commissioner for human rights and putting more resources into that important part of the mandate.
I want to close by underlining the importance of the NGO role, both Canadian NGOs, including the United Nations Association of Canada, and international NGOs, as we approach this 50th anniversary of the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to introduce this bill today amending the Criminal Code, the Young Offenders Act and the Corrections and Conditional Release Act.
The bill will close a significant loophole in sentencing laws. It will lower the age of application of the Young Offenders Act, outlaw the crack houses, provide for stiffer bail procedures, deny statutory release to repeat serious offenders and allow judicially ordered blood tests of those accused of rape.
I want to acknowledge the support and constructive input of my colleague in the House, the hon. member for Red Deer, the constructive input of colleagues in my caucus, colleagues on the justice committee and representatives of victims groups, all who have contributed to the drafting of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present to this House a petition that was collected by Lynne Stoner of Dorchester Road in Niagara Falls. She has collected petitions of individuals numbering 6,400. These people are from all across the Niagara peninsula. These 6,400 individuals, most of whom are women, because of the senseless, needless and violent deaths of women all across this country are asking that this Parliament pass an anti-stalking law. I
am pleased to say that there is now before Parliament an anti-stalking law.
I appreciate all the time and effort that went into putting together this petition. I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all colleagues of the House that I will do everything that I can and I urge other hon. members to join me in making sure an anti-stalking law is in place before we go home for the summer.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition on behalf of a group of constituents of mine who humbly call upon Parliament to enact legislation which will allow a referendum of the people binding upon Parliament to accept or reject two official languages, English and French, for the government and the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have here hundreds of petitions from Ontario against the North American free trade agreement. Some of these petitions come from the Goderich-Kincardine area, including such places as Blyth, up that peninsula, but the vast bulk of these petitions come from my constituents in Essex-Windsor.
They were collected throughout the constituency. They reflect the very strong view of my constituents in Essex-Windsor that this North American free trade agreement will cause Canadians to lose more jobs, that if implemented the free trade deal with result in further restrictions being placed on the ability of Canada's federal, provincial and territorial governments now and in the future from assisting Canadian industry, conserving Canadian natural resources for Canadian benefit and advancing needed social programs.
Therefore, the petitioners call upon the House to reject the legislation in front of the House today implementing the North American free trade arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of presenting a number of petitions today.
The first petition is signed by residents of Burnaby, Vancouver and other parts of British Columbia. It notes that two young Canadians, Christine Lamont and David Spencer, who have been sentenced to 28 years each in a Brazilian prison have suffered grave miscarriages of justice in Brazilian prisons and in the courts, that the cumulative effect of these irregularities provides ample
May 27, 1993

ground for the Government of Canada to seek a remedy and the only effective remedy from this punishment is for Canada to request expulsion in accordance with Brazilian law.
Therefore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to request the Government of Brazil to expel Christine Lamont and David Spencer and return them to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have another set of petitions which are signed again by residents of my own constituency of Burnaby- Kingsway as well as New Westminster and other parts of the lower mainland of British Columbia collected in particular by Mr. Raghbir Jawandha, Phin Malthe and Jose Gomez.
These petitions note that the federal government through Immigration Canada is in the process of eliminating services now available to the public. The New Westminster Canada Immigration Centre provides good local service which will be withdrawn to a less efficient, less accessible and already overworked Vancouver Canada Immigration Centre.
As a result of the hardship imposed, the petitioners call upon Parliament to demand that the government not eliminate in-person services and not close local Immigration Canada offices across the country.

Mr. Speaker, next I have petitions which are signed by several thousand Canadians from coast to coast to coast on the subject of using animals in tests.
They note that tests and experiments are presently being made on animals in schools, colleges, universities and hospitals, as well as in industrial and commercial laboratories of all kinds.
The petitioners urge Parliament to totally and complete abolish all tests and experiments using live animals
Routine Proceedings
in the pretext of relating observations to humans, as such practices are not only cruel, unnecessary, unjustifiable, unreliable and morally wrong, but they invariably generate misleading concepts and dangerous results which are most damaging to the health of Canadians as well as to that of citizens from every country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have several petitions from over 700 Okanagan Centre residents to go with several thousand names which have been presented to the Clerk.
They are petitioning the House of Commons to consider amending the Criminal Code of Canada so that violent and degrading material such as the serial killer board game can be kept from being distributed in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a second petition with several thousand names from residents of my riding of Okanagan Centre who are concerned that the post office is closing and privatizing post offices. Canada Post has stated that the Kelowna post offices will be closed during 1993.
Your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to stop these closures and the privatization of postal services, and to ensure that the citizens and taxpayers of Kelowna, British Columbia have full service post offices which are directly run by the Canada Post Corporation.
I may add that the Kelowna post office has closed and it is anticipated the other two to be closed are in Rutland and Westbank. The petitioners are hoping that these two post offices will be saved.

Mr. Speaker, today I am presenting another petition signed by constituents of mine who are concerned about the North American free trade agreement.
On this day when Parliament is debating for the last time the North American free trade agreement legisla-

May 27, 1993
Routine Proceedings
tion before the cold guillotine of closure comes down on it, I would like to present this petition to Parliament.
The petitioners state that the current Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement sharply reduces the power of all Canadian governments to develop the Canadian economy. They note that more than 400,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since the free trade agreement became law in 1989. They also state that if implemented, the North American free trade agreement will cause even more jobs to be lost.
Therefore the petitioners call upon this House to reject the proposed North American free trade agreement and recommend to government that it use the FTA's termination clause to end the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
The names on this petition bring the total to some several hundred that have been collected in my constituency in only the last few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my pleasure to present this petition.
It is signed by many residents from Creston, Wynndel and Erickson in my riding of Kootenay East. They state that the proposed North American free trade agreement has resulted in ever greater trade concessions being demanded of Canada; that the Canadian Constitution requires a general federal election before Januaiy 1, 1994, the date on which the North American free trade agreement is scheduled to come into force.
Therefore we call upon the House to reject the proposed North American free trade agreement and to recommend to the government that it use the termination clause to end the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by my constituents in the Yukon who wish to draw to the attention of Parliament their concern that the goods and services tax should not apply to certain products because they are necessities.
My constituents particularly refer to women's sanitary products. They respectfully suggest that the government
should withdraw the GST from those articles which constitute a necessity for women.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the opportunity to speak in this debate.
It is very important legislation. It is legislation about the future of our country. The NAFTA is a comprehensive agreement that builds on the progress we have already made to date in the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. The NAFTA improves on our access to the United States market. It also opens up access in a very important way to the fast-growing Mexican market.
The agreement is about growth and prosperity. Opponents of trade often suggest that the benefits for one country come at the expense of another.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
I guess, Mr. Speaker, I said something that has twitched a nerve end.
Expanded trade and investment benefits all those who engage in it. By specializing in what we do best we

Government Orders
improve our productivity and increase our wealth. I have said on many occasions that it is important for us to get as many companies as possible involved in international markets. That is what the free trade agreements we have entered into will do.
The reason I say that is if companies are involved day in and day out in meeting the world competition they are going to be better companies for it. They are going to be able to generate more business in Canada, more business internationally, and be there in a much stronger way as we go through the normal ups and downs that are bound to happen in any economy.
With free trade liberalization we both preserve and create jobs and improve the prospects for Canadian companies to compete successfully world-wide. As we improve our productivity, our competitiveness, in dealing first with the United States and now in the NAFTA with Mexico, it will put us in a stronger position to take on the competition in the Far East, in Europe, or in central and eastern Europe. This is an essential objective of a free trade agreement. This is the proven strategy for growth and for improvements in our standard of living here in Canada.
The results of the free trade agreement to date are powerful. The figures speak for themselves. Canadian merchandise trade surplus with the United States rose 13.6 per cent last year over the previous year. Our merchandise trade surplus with the United States last year was $17.7 billion. That compares with $13.8 billion in 1988, the year before the free trade agreement came into force.
Looking behind those numbers you can see that the exports to the United States were up 13.5 per cent last year in a year when the U.S. economy grew at about 5 per cent. So far this year we can see that the trend is continuing, as exports to the United States in the first quarter compared to the same period last year were up 23 per cent. It is clear that it is the export business that has been assisted in such a major way by the free trade agreement which is driving the recovery in this country out of the recession we came out of a couple of years ago.
Exports are the engines of growth in Canada today. A C.D. Howe Institute analysis shows that in the first three years of the free trade agreement, those products which are benefiting the most from this increase in exports are
those that have received the greatest amount of trade liberalization and the greatest reduction in their tariffs going into the United States market.
I have heard members opposite on a number of occasions say that what we should be doing is generating more value-added manufacturing. That is precisely what the free trade agreement is doing. As we drop the tariffs on value-added products going into the United States market, it creates a manufacturing base for us in Canada. That is why we have seen a substantial increase in value-added products going into the United States market.
It is interesting to see that in the very high-tech areas, like telecommunications or aerospace, such as our exports in the first four years were up something like 60 per cent, but coming the other way interestingly, the U.S. exports into Canada in these products were up about 12 per cent.
Clearly we have gained market share and the free trade agreement has been a veiy important element of gaining that market share.
We have all said on many occasions in this House that Canada is a trading nation and there is no doubt about that. But our goal as a government has been to protect today's markets and to open up the markets of tomorrow. It is with this aim that we are pushing forward with an ambitious result in the Uruguay round at the multilateral trade negotiations. We achieved this through the negotiation of the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement and now we have consolidated and improved upon this by negotiating the North American free trade agreement.
Let us look again at what this agreement does for Canada. It improves the already good access that we have into the United States market. It gives us preferential access to a growing and dynamic Mexican market, a young market, a market that is growing faster than that of the United States or Canada. It is a market we should be in. I should say we are already because the publicity and the interest that the NAFTA has generated is already generating some activity in Mexico.
Our exports last year were up 35 per cent. We have seen an increase in business visitors from 1,000 in 1990, to 2,000 in 1991, to 4,500 in 1992 and that trend is continuing.
May 27, 1993

It also ensures that Canada remains a preferred location for investment, investment by both foreign investors as well as Canadian investors. As they see that we have this better access to the United States and considerably improved access to Mexico, they are being drawn into using Canada as a base for their operations for the total North American market.
Our wealth and growth prospects depend on access to world markets. We are a small market in terms of population. Our access to outside markets underpins our economy and standard of living, and that is why we negotiated the free trade agreement with the United States. That is why we have also negotiated the North American free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico.
The U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement laid a foundation for Canadian prosperity. At a time of rising protectionist pressures throughout the world, not least of which was in the United States, Canada is in the enviable position of having through the FTA preferential access to the United States market.
The NAFTA preserves the benefits of the FTA. It ensures that Canada remains a prime investment location and it provides continued protection for key domestic areas, including our cultural industries, public education, health and social services, including child care.

The NAFTA substantially expands the benefits of the FTA. After four years of experience with the FTA we had the opportunity to make improvements and broaden the coverage in such areas as intellectual property protection and land transportation. We now have clearer rules for regulating Canada-United States trade, and new market access in the U.S. in areas not covered by the Canada-United States FTA. These improvements give Canadian businesses new opportunities in the U.S. and Mexico and place Canadian business on an even sounder footing for expanding our exports in important offshore markets.

Let me review some of the major new areas covered by the North American free trade agreement. One is duty drawback. This provision allows Canadian exporters to be refunded for the tariff that is paid on business inputs, products that they use in the production of their own
Government Orders
manufactured products that are later exported. This was to be eliminated under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement next January, but under the NAFTA we have extended this deadline for two years. More important, new rules give certain permanent duty drawback rights for exporters who do not meet the NAFTA rules of origin.
The NAFTA rules of origin improve on those of the FTA. They are clearer and more predictable. That is a real benefit to Canadian exporters and potential investors in Canada. For many products the necessity of calculating content has simply been eliminated and replaced by the more precise tariff shift rules.
For most products still subject to a content requirement, there are two possible calculations from which an exporter can choose, at least one of which is considerably simpler than the one that is available now under the FTA.
Regulations will be established to ensure that Canadian, U.S. and Mexican customs officials apply the rules uniformly.
Finally, advance rulings on the origin of goods to be traded within the NAFTA area will further minimize the uncertainties for traders and investors.

The NAFTA maintains and improves upon the FTA's dispute settlement provisions.
The right Canada achieved in the FTA to take final appeals of countervail and dumping cases to a binational, impartial panel is clearly recognized in the NAFTA. Business people who have been subjected to the U.S. trade remedies system tell me that this dispute settlement procedure is a key asset of the FTA and one envied by those who do not have it.
The NAFTA gives Canadian service sector businesses new access to the North American market. It expands to services the basic obligations of national treatment which has long been applied to goods through the GATT and other trade agreements.
A signatory country cannot require that a service firm from a NAFTA country establish or maintain a local presence as a precondition for access to its market; this means that Canadian firms can provide services to the U.S. and Mexican market from Canada.

May 27, 1993
Government Orders

Under its temporaiy entry provisions the NAFTA opens up cross-border entry for over 60 professions. As Mexico continues to develop it will need professional consulting assistance in the areas of telecommunications, utilities, land transportation services and consulting engineering. These are all areas in which Canadians excel.
Additional benefits are achieved in financial services. Under the NAFTA Mexico's financial markets will be opened up to Canadian banking, insurance and securities firms. This will allow Canadian financial institutions to participate in the rapidly expanding Mexican economy, a promising market that was closed to us until the negotiation of the NAFTA.
In another improvement on the FTA the NAFTA financial services obligations are covered by the agreement's general disputes settlement procedures. The FTA did not include provisions on land transportation. This has been rectified. Under the NAFTA a Canadian trucker can now unload in the United States, reload there, go to Mexico and haul back a cargo to the United States and Canada. At the same time we have maintained our cabotage rights.
The investment provisions of the NAFTA are another example where the FTA provisions were expanded offering to Canadian investors a more secure footing in the North American marketplace and securing for the future, their preferential access to Mexico. For additional security, disputes between an investor from a NAFTA country and another NAFTA country may be settled at the investor's options by international arbitration. Canada meanwhile maintains its rights to review foreign takeovers.
Canadian businesses gain new intellectual property protection in the NAFTA consistent with international rules that have developed in the Uruguay round negotiations. As the Canadian economy moves into higher value-added, knowledge-based growth areas, this protection for copyrights, patents, trade marks and trade secrets will protect our ability to expand into the NAFTA area. This in turn will make us a more competitive and attractive place to do business and create higher paying jobs.
It will clearly attract more investment into Canada as we have seen in the pharmaceutical area where over $700 million of investment has been attracted into Canada because of those changes that have been brought about by this government, consistent with the Uruguay round and the NAFTA.
The government procurement provisions of the NAFTA significantly expand the coverage contained in the FTA. The NAFTA adds about $50 billion in covered procurement to what was already opened in competitive bidding under the GATT and the FTA. Canadian businesses will have the opportunity to bid on contracts from such major buyers as the U.S. Corps of Engineers and the Mexican Pemex Corporation which together buy over $15 billion in goods and services each year.
I know my friends opposite do not like to hear about these positive changes to the NAFTA compared to what we have now. These changes to the NAFTA are going to generate job and investment opportunities in Canada.
They are going to result in a change for the better in this country that will reduce the unemployment rate and improve the competitive position of Canadian business. I know that is a major disappointment to my friends opposite. They can see that as the economy improves their opportunities to come to this side of the House are long gone.
I am sorry to have to say that. That is why I see the number of long faces on that side of the House. These NAFTA achievements represent new opportunities open to Canadians in the United States as well as in Mexico.

Canada to sell into the Mexican market. This is a very important fact for Canadian auto workers in Canada. The opportunities this man spoke about were virtually closed to Canadian automotive producers before Mexico agreed in the NAFTA to eliminate its automotive decree.
This is only a very partial list. Canadians can compete around the world and we can compete in Mexico. The NAFTA gives us an advantage over all non-NAFTA countries that allows us to take advantage of these opportunities in Mexico. It is an advantage we must seize.
Trade is not an end in itself, but it is a means to an end. [DOT]The ultimate end is prosperity offered by an efficient economy that generates the wealth necessary for Canadians to pay for the social programs they demand and expect to pay for such as public education, to create higher paying jobs and underwrite continued future improvements in our standard of living and our quality of life.
We are currently negotiating side deals on the environment and labour. Canada pressed for strong improvements in these areas during the original negotiations and I brought this forward in February 1992. We are fully committed to working with our NAFTA partners to promote the highest possible level of co-operation in these important areas. We do however have to get these agreements right. They have to work.
For that reason the Canadian position will continue to oppose the use of trade sanctions to enforce compliance. We will insist instead on mechanisms that promote co-operation and certainty instead of confrontation and uncertainty.
Some hon. members opposite contend that the government is losing its negotiating leverage by proceeding with Bill C-115 before the side agreements are concluded. The fact is that Bill C-115 is not relevant to the achievement of Canada's objectives in the side agreements. The NAFTA is a good deal for Canada with or without the side agreements, but we are working hard for good agreements on environment and labour co-operation. However, the value of NAFTA to Canada is not conditional upon the conclusion of these additional
agreements. All that delaying or implementing legislation would accomplish-perversely-would be to deprive Canadian businesses and their workers of the certainty needed to finalize plans for taking advantage of the many opportunities opened up by the NAFTA.
We are also not prepared to see Canadians misled by misrepresentations of about the NAFTA. We have been exposing these myths. We will continue to expose these myths. The NAFTA does not give the United States or Mexico any rights to exploit our water. Claims to the contrary are absurd puffery. Our 1987 federal water policy explicitly prohibits large scale exports of water by inter-basin transfer or diversion and nothing in the NAFTA or any other trade agreement forces Canada to exploit our water resources or to export our water. Until water enters commerce as a good, it is not covered by the NAFTA or any other trade agreement. The bottom line is that Canadian governments, both now and under the NAFTA, have the freedom of action required to regulate the exploitation of our water resources.
The NAFTA does not threaten Canadian jobs. I will tell what does threaten Canadian jobs: low productivity, recession battered markets, protectionist trade barriers, inflation driven prices, volatile exchange rates, inwardlooking business plans as well as inward-looking politicians. All of these are what threatens Canadian jobs. The NAFTA does not create unfair competition. Canada is already competing against low wage countries as well as high wage countries throughout the world. Their markets are our hope for the future.

When he wanted to build the Seaway at one time the Americans did not want to co-operate. C. D. Howe did not go fishing with the president. He told the Americans that if they did not want to participate then Canada could do it alone. That is the way a Liberal government handles a tough situation.
Look at what is happening today. We are going to vote on a bill today to approve the NAFTA. When the deal was made it was approved in the dying hours of President Bush's term and now we are approving it in the dying hours of the Prime Minister. Of course we are free traders. We know that we have to trade. We know that Canada has always been the biggest trading nation in the world per capita. Yes, we have been that.
When it passed the FTA it said that we would have guaranteed access to the American market. Less than a month ago I was in Hamilton and met with the representative of Stelco. They decide in the United States under what conditions we should operate in Canada and they presume that it should cost us that much and we cannot prove the contrary.
What we want is real access. What we want is a definition of what a subsidy is. What we want is a definition of what dumping is. When we have these rules in place we will compete, but we must have the rules and we must have a commitment that the rules will be respected. That is the problem with this deal.
I am not like the New Democrats. We are not like them. We do not want to build a wall around Canada that is not what we want. We know that Canadians can compete, but we must have rules. We have to know exactly what can be done and after that we will adjust.

At the last minute, in the middle of the negotiation with the United States, it says: "Let us pass the bill". When it has to go to the negotiating table it does not want to have one little tool with which to negotiate. It surrenders before the beginning of the fight. That is why we are opposing the process. We are opposing the process because it makes no sense. We should postpone that and review it after the election.
We believe we will be the government and we have some concrete proposals. Depending on who they are talking to, the NDP say just scrap the agreement. When
the leader of the New Democratic Party spoke with The Financial Post, she said she wants to renegotiate the deal. That makes sense. But after she met with her radical friends she changed her mind.
The Liberal Party has a clear position. We cannot go back to square one. It is very naive to think we can go back to square one.

Two of the conditions have been picked up by President Clinton. We were the first to talk about renegotiating the environmental conditions and the labour conditions. We have been talking about them for two years and President Clinton picked them up.

What is wrong with that? If it is good enough for the Mexicans, it should be good enough for the Canadians. I do not think it would be a difficult negotiation.
What will be the answer that the Americans give us? Why treat Canada differently from the Mexicans if we are supposed to be three partners in a deal? I do not think there will be a very difficult argument.
I mentioned to the minister earlier that the next two conditions we want to renegotiate are what a subsidy is and what dumping is? We have to know that. We have had more problems with our trade relations with the United States since this government claimed it obtained access for Canadian goods in the United States.
May 27, 1993

Wheat, softwood lumber, pork, cars-there are many more-magnesium, lobsters. Every time it is a new problem. Because we can access their market, can compete in their market, the Americans use their own rules. They claim it is a subsidy. They claim it is dumping. In the end they sock it to us and that becomes harassment. What we need is a clear definition of what is a subsidy and what is dumping.
There is a clause in the FTA which says that in the seven years after the implementation of the FTA, we have to conclude negotiations on what is a subsidy and what is dumping. There is a commitment by the Americans to the Canadian government that in the seven years after the implementation of the FTA they will renegotiate the conditions of dumping and subsidy.
Will the Americans say we are not reasonable when we ask them to respect the promise they put in the agreement at that time?
When we have a good definition of what a subsidy is and what dumping is, we will have a deal and I will tell the Canadian people that we will have to compete and we can compete. We have always been good at competing but we have to have some rules.
For instance there is no use playing hockey if in the middle of a period the other coach decides his team will play eight against five. We know it is five players plus a goalie. No more. That is the rule. We play according to the rules, but the Americans change the rules according to their own desires. This is not free trade. This is not access to trade in United States.
Therefore we have to have new negotiations and we will have new negotiations. A lot of people ask me what guarantees I have that the Americans will want to renegotiate. I say that if it was a bad deal for the Americans, they would want to renegotiate. They would want to have a better deal for themselves.
Why do members opposite sometimes ask: Do they want to renegotiate? It is very easy. It is because it is a very good deal for them. If it is a very good deal for them they will want to keep as much of a good deal as possible. They will sit down with us and we will negotiate what they want to negotiate such as conditions on labour and environment if that is not finished.

speechtext:
At the end of a mandate people get nervous. I was saying that the government is making a big mistake because it is not serving the best interests of Canada at this time when Mexico, the United States and Canada are negotiating environmental and labour side agreements.
Last week's discussions will have a major impact on the content of NAFTA because the Americans clearly stated that they reserved the right to change the rules of access to the American market if any of the participating countries did not meet the conditions with respect to labour and the environment. What this means is a direct negation of the will expressed by the three countries to ensure each partner had free access to the others' markets all the time. This does constitute a radical change to NAFTA.
The government wants to rush this deal through at the eleventh hour, just a few months or weeks before an election, when they know full well that, in all likelihood, they will no longer be the government by the end of the year. That is abuse of power, and they will pay dearly for it. In fact, the Canadian people will let them know that at election time.

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
I think that when you are at the end of a mandate as they are you should try not to cause political trouble just to score political points like the Tories are doing right now. Obviously, what the Conservative Party is trying to do right now is cause trouble for the new government that we will have in October. They have no regard whatsoever for the needs of the Canadian people and that is the saddest part of it all right now. The negotiations are not over. This government is ramming through this bill while Mexico has not even introduced its own legislation and President Clinton has clearly stated that he will not introduce legislation in Congress until such time as a side agreement on environmental and labour issues has been signed.
It is obvious to whoever reads careffully American newspapers these days that this bill will not go to the U.S. Congress before early or late fall. We should do the same thing here in Canada. After the election, we will still have two and a half months to act on this and at that time the Canadian Parliament will have the authority and duty to decide whether Canadian interests were afforded sufficient protection during negotiations and whether or not to proceed with proclamation, but not before making sure that Canadian interests are well protected. We have clearly stated what is required to protect Canadian interests. As I said before, the conditions are a new round of negotiations on subsidies, dumping, the same conditions with respect to energy as set by Mexico and the two things President Clinton himself is trying to change and that we have been wanting to change for two years now, that is the provisions relating to environmental and labour issues.
Given that the debate is not over and that it is now clear that the government is only trying to make itself look good or to cause embarrassment while totally disregarding the national interest-

I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-115, an act to implement the North American Free Trade Agreement be not now read a third time, but that it be read a third time this day six months hence".

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us be very clear from the beginning of this debate on the North American free trade agreement that this is not just another commercial agreement. This is the sellout of Canada.
I do not make that statement lightly and I intend in my comments today to show why this is so. NAFTA is a sellout of Canadian jobs, a betrayal of Canadian families and only one of the many trade options from which Canadians can choose.
This is very important for all Canadians. All Canadians must believe that this has an effect on their lives and it will affect every man, woman and child in Canada.

There has not been in this country a true debate on NAFTA. I am upset about this debate not only because Canadians were not given a chance to be heard, but also because the government did not listen to what Canadians had to say about this trade agreement.
NAFTA is the final gasp of a government that knows it cannot pass legislation by going to the people so it imposes legislation by circumventing the people. That is shameful.
Let me assure this departing government that this injustice will not be forgotten by Canadians. Canadians understand what is at stake with NAFTA. It is no less than the economic constitution of this country. By that I mean NAFTA has profound implications for the future of Canada. It will determine how we develop our economy. It will determine how we govern ourselves. It will determine how we care for each other. It will determine what kind of society we leave our children, and with NAFTA none of those implications is positive.
It is important to remember that NAFTA is not about more freedom for citizens but more freedom for capital to move where it wants, when it wants, without restriction and without responsibility to those who create the wealth of the country, the working people.
The rates of unemployment we have seen are disastrous for the country. There is only one thing that can be said about them. Canada works when Canadians are
May 27, 1993

Government Orders
working. That must be our goal. That is why trade arrangements must be about bettering the lives of working people. A trade policy should exist to serve the people. People do not exist to serve trade.
The Conservative government argues that NAFTA will improve the lives of Canadians. Nothing in this deal or nothing in our experience with the Canada-U.S. trade agreement would lead anyone to believe that NAFTA could benefit Canadian families. I say to the government to get out of its offices in Ottawa and sit down at kitchen tables with families across the country. Just go as far as Scarborough and sit down with those 3,000 men and women who lost their jobs at a company moving south. They will tell the government what they think about bad trade deals and the destruction they have wrought for Canadian families.
As I said earlier the U.S.-Canada deal has spelled great unemployment as one factory after another shuts down and heads south. Almost 500,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since 1988: for example, 22,000 in the furniture sector, 12,000 in textiles, 42,000 in clothing, 23,000 in plastics, 20,000 in auto parts, 30,000 in machinery, and 23,000 in printing and business.
Statistics alone do not tell of the hardships. They do not tell the real story. It is people like Gary St. Laurent who used to be president of the union at Kelsey-Hayes, a wheel making plant in Windsor who tell the real story. Until it closed down three years ago he was working productively and his family was working productively. However his company was another fatality of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement. At the Ontario government's public hearings on NAFTA this spring Mr. St. Laurent described his unemployed neighbours this way:
They've lost their homes. They've lost their cars. They've lost their
families.
He went on to say:
We've had at least three suicides at Kelsey-Hayes since we went
down in 1990.
We cannot ignore the human cost of what this government's corporate agenda has done to Canada. No government, no political party, has a right to inflict such suffering on the very people it was elected to serve.

Among other things, NAFTA will add to the number of jobs already lost through the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States. I want to say a word about one of the most important provisions of NAFTA which will result in an event greater number of Canadian jobs being exported abroad.
This provision deals with the changes made to the rules of origin. These changes will undermine the very foundation of the Auto Pact for the automobile industry. Indeed, the Auto Pact guaranteed a Canadian content in the production of automobiles. It provided some protection for our automobile industry by specifying that a certain number of vehicles had to be assembled in Canada. The Auto Pact also provided that, for each vehicle, a certain number of parts had to be made here in Canada.
With NAFTA, there is no longer this kind of protection for our automobile industry. There is a provision saying that 62 per cent of vehicles will have to have a North American content. But all the work related to this North American content could very well be done in Mexico or in the United States. There is no provision to the effect that part of this content must come from Canada. Moreover, NAFTA will forever keep us from being able to sign an auto pact with the auto makers of Japan or any other country.

Changes to the rules of origin could also ruin our clothing industry. We have seen many lay-offs in the textile industry. They will have and have had an especially brutal effect on women, mostly older and immigrant women, many of whom are the vast majority of workers in this industry. As it is the combined pressures of the U.S.-Canada trade deal and the Maquiladoras have devastated our clothing industry. However they have done more than that. They have done more than kill thousands of jobs.
In Canada these pressures have led to an insidious new cottage industry in Canada called home work. Here women are fired from the clothing factory and contracted to sew at home for less than minimum wages, without benefits, without Canada Pension Plan, without

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
unemployment insurance and without workers' compensation. Let me emphasize that this is happening in our own country. It is a concrete example of how people can be forced to serve trade if trade is not used to serve people.
NAFTA jeopardizes other industries and services such as telecommunications and data processing, again areas where women are the majority of workers. This suggests the government has never considered, examined or cared about how this deal would affect women. Nothing in this agreement or in government policy improves women's job prospects or working conditions. There is no retraining, no bridging programs, no child care.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to move from the issue of safety for Canadian families to that of the repercussions of NAFTA on the security of our country, its resources, its programs and its sovereignty. Once again, NAFTA affects all Canadians. This trade agreement is even more deplorable than the free trade agreement with the United States, because we will have even less control over tariffs and the exports of our energy resources.
NAFTA opens the door to massive exports of Canadian water, even in times of shortage in our own country. Because of this trade agreement, we will no longer be able to insist that our trains, our trucks and our buses transport Canadian goods on Canadian soil.
NAFTA would codify the Conservative drug patent legislation and thereby reinforce the control of multinational companies over our health plan.

NAFTA further restricts our economic options such as regulating foreign investment, promoting regional development and developing an industrial strategy for Canada. It undermines our ability to challenge arbitrary U.S. trade laws.
It interferes with our right to appeal to GATT and eliminates any possibility of negotiating a subsidies code.
In a very serious area, NAFTA weakens our ability to establish Crown corporations, corporations in the public interest with social goals such as conserving energy and providing airline service to remote communities. This does not just affect the federal government, this affects provincial governments.
NAFTA is so far reaching that it binds the provinces as well from establishing these kinds of corporations that could indeed be and have in the past been in the public interest.
Finally, NAFTA does nothing to slow down, never mind reverse, free trade's race to the bottom on wages, work place safety and environmental standards. Let me illustrate with an example. The average wage of a Canadian worker is $13.10 an hour. For Americans it is about $12.50 a hour but if you went to many states with no minimum wage, it would be much less. It could be as low as $4 or $5 an hour.
For Mexicans it is barely $1 an hour. Given that pattern, it is not hard to figure out where Canadian wages and Canadian jobs are heading under NAFTA. Think of this. Someone said to me the other day: "You know, we have all this pressure to take less wages, less benefits, reduce safety standards in the work place, reduce environmental standards, and if our wages keep going down, who is going to buy these products?" Who is going to buy these products when workers have less and less wages to do so?
It just makes common sense that the interests of the multinational companies are not the interests of the ordinary working people in any of the three countries party to this agreement.
When the government cannot defend NAFTA on the basis of what it will do for Canadian workers and Canadian families, it resorts to accusing opponents of not wanting to improve the lives of Mexican workers and their families. Nothing can be further from the truth as far as this party is concerned. Believe me if this trade agreement was based on the ability and the objectives of increasing the living standards and working standards, the health and safety standards and the environmental standards of Mexican workers, the New Democrats would be first in line to support it.
The reality is that it is not the interest of the people of any of the three countries who are dealt with in this agreement. It is the interests of transferring accountability from elected governments to unelected, unaccountable multinational corporations which will make the decisions.
People think that this is somehow fanciful and could not happen. I would like to remind people of history and of Central America where throughout history the United Fruit Growers basically ran many countries in Central
May 27, 1993

America. When things did not go the way they wanted, they asked the American army to come in to take care of it. That is what the corporate agenda is all about. Who gets to make the decisions?
This government has given decisions about health care and particularly drug care over to the large multinationals, not to Canadians. This government has transferred decision-making in many areas through its program of deregulation.
NAFTA is simply an extension of what this government has already put in place. It is blatant dishonesty and hypocrisy on the part of the government to say that NAFTA is simply to aid Mexican workers and to say that those who are opposed to NAFTA do not want to.
The Wall Street Journal, which I think is one of the Conservative Party's favourite sources of information, has described Mexico's free trade zones as "helping to turn much of the border region into a sink hole of abysmal living conditions and environmental degradation".
The same journal also says that child labour, even in hazardous jobs, is rampant in Mexico. NAFTA will do nothing to outlaw the exploitation of society's most vulnerable members, its children.
This government can stand in its place and say: "We want to help the Mexican people". Well, the first step is to stop NAFTA now.
Many Canadians have read of the environmental conditions in the Maquiladoras and how that has affected parts of Texas. They have read the stories about Brownsville, Texas and indeed about families in the Maquiladoras who were suffering from the results of environmental degradation. Children were bom disfigured and disabled. We cannot be ignorant of the fact that environmental conditions have a profound effect on our whole society. A poor environment leads to the degradation of the economy. It leads to health problems. It increases health care costs. Look to eastern Europe where we saw that the ruthless exploitation of the people and the industries leading to massive environmental problems simply destroyed the economy.
Government Orders
This government has it all wrong. It should be thinking of the people instead of the corporations. Then it would be building a true economy.
Another argument often used is that NAFTA will bring higher wages to Mexican workers. I would like to point out one fact. Despite rising investment in Mexico throughout the Maquiladoras in the 1980s manufacturing wages fell by 25 per cent. They did not go up, they fell by 25 per cent. Equally as serious, Mexican workers who demanded better pay risked their lives.
According to Southam News correspondent Dave Todd: "When pay and benefits at Ford's main Mexican plant were cut in half in 1990 armed thugs were brought in to stifle a union revolt. The Mexican government refused to prosecute anyone for the assaults that resulted in the death of one worker and the wounding of eight others".
The New Democratic Party knows that NAFTA will not improve the lives of ordinary Mexicans. We know that NAFTA will not improve the lives of working people in Canada. Why continue? Why continue with an agreement, as we have seen from the examples of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, that will cost Canadians jobs and devastate communities?
There are options. This government has options and Canadians have options. I know the government will not take any options so I prefer to speak directly to the Canadian people because there are things that will improve their lives. Our party believes that a policy that puts fair trade with many nations before free trade with a few is the policy that will lead us successfully into the 21st century.
The government is fond of saying that anyone who opposes its trade arrangements wants to put a wall up around Canada. I heard the hon. Leader of the Opposition today say that the New Democratic Party wants to put a wall up around Canada. They are wrong. It is quite the opposite. What they want to do is put a wall up around North America. We want to be open to the world. We want to assist those countries that need trade with Canada and we want to be truly a part of the international community.
We do propose an alternative. It is not the alternative of the Liberals, which is that they are really going to talk against NAFTA but they will probably implement it if they are government. We have never heard them say that they would not implement it. They said that they would renegotiate. I happen to remember when the hon.

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
Leader of the Opposition went to the United States. He spoke to President Bush about renegotiation. President Bush laughed, sent him home and said forget it, there was no renegotiation clause in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
There are alternatives. I did not hear of any alternatives at all from the Liberal Party today. I would like to outline briefly our alternatives.
Our trade strategy has three pillars: First, a broad, steady and planned reduction of tariffs through the GATT. We do not think the GATT is perfect. In fact I think there are many things that we would work for as a party to change in the GATT. It is a multilateral accord with 108 member countries. We would work for a planned reduction of tariffs through the GATT.
Second, we would work toward more sectoral agreements, such as the auto pact. We would look for sectoral agreements in steel. I think it is worth mentioning that sectoral agreements are certainly in the interests of Canadians, but they are of interest to our trading partners as well. It is a balanced approach where countries working together can in fact develop agreements that are in the interests of both parties or all parties.
The third pillar is the exploration of untapped markets in Europe, the Pacific rim and Latin America, markets that Canada has not attempted with any vigour to enter.
At the same time, our strategy would give Canadian workers a fair chance at participating in the global economy. That means more than taking the time to adjust, retrain and retool, although that is important, but it also means negotiating a charter of workers' rights such as the European Community has done. It means as well being ready to respond when any firm violates basic standards on pollution, labour and human rights.
The New Democratic trade strategy is both orderly and outward looking. Unlike the one-sided Tory trade deals, our vision satisfies both sides of the equation. It would guarantee Canadian businesses the market access they simply are not assured under the FTA or under NAFTA. We would see to this by helping companies to develop opportunities in new and expanding markets.
This strategy is a solid alternative to NAFTA and it is spelled out in the New Democratic Party's plan for jobs.
A couple of months ago we brought out a jobs plan where we talked about the strategies for developing a Canadian economy, and by doing so getting Canadians back working and reducing our deficit. If I might say so for those watching, it is possible to get our jobs plan by calling 1-800-565-2122. Our plan for Canada is free, but ignoring it I believe has an incalculable cost.
Despite the government's effort to stifle debate on this bill, it has become clear where political parties stand. We are really talking here about how we will go forward into the 21st century. I suspect there are many of us at this time of year who are speaking to graduating classes in high schools. These are the young people who really will be the 21st century adults.
We in this century have no right to tie their hands to ensure that they will not get jobs. We have a responsibility to provide alternatives in developing the Canadian economy that include investments in education, research, jobs and in ensuring that Canada does not go in to the 21st century as the 51st state. Our party does not see that as the future of Canada.
Where do the political parties stand? The Conservatives, of course, do not really have any proof but they wistfully continue to believe that NAFTA should go ahead despite the facts, and they intend to impose this on Canadians in their last days in government.
The Liberals have several positions. They criticize NAFTA but refuse to say whether or not they would actually implement it. The Leader of the Opposition has said he expects to form the government next time but Canadians have a right to know whether he also expects not to ratify NAFTA. That should be his responsibility.
The Liberals talk very favourably about parallel accords knowing full well that NAFTA has many provisions that are so flawed that parallel accords could not correct them. Parallel accords do not touch the sell-out of our energy resources, our water or our inability to deal with foreign investment. They do not touch any of those things.
May 27, 1993

The Liberals talk about renegotiating but even President Clinton, as did President Bush before him, said he will not open the accord itself. There was an opportunity in this House to defeat NAFTA. It is not going to be defeated today. Let us be honest. We are going to be voting on the NAFTA. The Conservative Party will have its people here. It has a majority government and intends to ram it through.
At second reading of this bill it could have been defeated. The New Democratic Party was here in full strength. Only half the Liberals showed up. They voted against it but not enough members came to make sure they could really defeat it.
I have to ask Canadians where these people really stand. Their stand is: "We get to say no. We get to stand up for Canadians but boy, when it comes to the vote we make sure we are not there. We do not want to win. We want the Conservative government to do the work for us."
It is clear there is only one party in this House that really opposes the sell-out of Canada and that is the New Democratic Party. We intend to make it an election issue. There is only one party in this Chamber that will not sit back, will not run away, will not stay home and will not cut deals as Canada faces its biggest betrayal yet.
Only one party in this country will stand up and be counted on to defeat NAFTA and that is the New Democratic Party of Canada. We know that the government is determined to ram NAFTA through this afternoon, defying common sense and business sense. It is rushing to pass NAFTA before the negotiations are even finished. We have to say: Why this haste?
There are only two reasons I suppose. We have an outgoing Prime Minister who wants a monument to himself. We have an outgoing trade minister who wants a monument to himself. I suggest that we build them statues. It would be cheaper for Canadians than signing this deal and seeing it pass.
I have to wonder if it is not more serious than that. We remember during the talks on the U.S.-Canada trade deal that the dollar was at 75 cents and our exports were fairly healthy. But after the trade deal was signed and implemented the dollar shot up and really tied the hands of exporters in this country.
Government Orders
We have to ask why. We did not have to ask very far because a former Tory industry minister said he thought there was a gentlemen's agreement.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext: A deal.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
A deal. If there was a gentlemen's agreement to prop up the dollar at the insistence of the U.S. after the U.S.-Canada trade deal, what agreements have been made since then that Canadians do not know about? What commitments have been made that Canadians have not been privy to?
There is a nation out there beyond the bubble of Ottawa and Bay Street. We have lived through one bad trade deal already. Before it is extended to Mexico Canadians deserve to know the truth. Contrary to what some people may suggest I do not find that Canadians are apathetic. They are not S.O.B.s and they are not the enemies of Canada.
Canadians have had it with nine years of Conservative callousness and of not being listened to. They have had it with nine years of hearing that there are no choices.
I want to assure those Canadians that there is a choice in the upcoming election. The choice is between a government that lays down for the Americans and one that stands up for Canadians.
The choice is not about whether we work in harmony with our neighbour but whether we become our neighbour. The choice is not about whether we participate in the international community, but on whose terms we participate.
I am proud that this country is renowned for its tradition of peacekeeping rather than warmongering. I am proud to be a Canadian where health care is a right of citizenship and not a privilege for the well-to-do. I am proud of a Canada whose system of old age pensions has greatly reduced poverty among our elders. I am proud of a Canada where my culture can be reflected through its artists, writers and broadcasters. Above all, I am proud to be part of a Canada that is beginning in a very historic sense to recognize and value self-government for first nation's people.
These are unique features of Canada that we could very well be losing to yet another bad trade deal. How can we on the one hand support sovereignty for the founding peoples through self-government agreements

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
and on the other hand give away the sovereignty of all Canadian people through the NAFTA trade deal and a new economic constitution?

Governments have options, but so do Canadians. When you travel in our country you realize that people get together in their communities-whether it is religious groups with unions or farm organizations with women's groups-to regain control of their lives, their community and their country.

This year a fundamental choice will be made. Will Canadians elect a federal government that believes as New Democrats believe in all we have built together, or will Canada become by Conservative decree or Liberal neglect the 51st state? There is a choice and that is why the New Democratic Party looks forward to the next election. We never want to have to tell our grandchildren that when we had the opportunity to choose we did not take it. So we say no to NAFTA and yes to Canada.
