Mr. Speaker, I will not attempt to respond to the comments made by my colleague of the opposition, instead I want to take a positive approach during this debate at third reading, which I think should be the case when speaking at this stage on an important bill which will give Canada access to a market of 85 million people and which will make
sure that Canada is not side-lined by an agreement between the United States and Mexico.
When talking about 85 million consumers in Mexico, we talk about Mexican consumers whose buying-power is constantly increasing. NAFTA is fundamentally in the best interest of Canada. If Canadians do not sell goods and services produced here in Canada to foreign buyers, it will very simply result in the disappearance of one out of every four jobs in Canada.
It is with this in mind that Canada got involved in NAFTA negotiations, to protect the interests of Canadians and to automatically strengthen our position as exporters. We know that Mexico has one of the fastest growing and most promising markets in the world. As that country is becoming more industrialized, its demand for refined consumer products increases.
In the past, Canadians did not have ready access to this market. Most Mexican products, or close to 80 percent, already enter into Canada duty-free. Canadian exports to Mexico were and still are subjected to many duties and other trade barriers. Something had to be done. If Canada had done nothing, it would not have the access it needs in order to guarantee prosperity for all Canadians.
You will recall the debate on free trade when months of fear mongering by the opposition made Canadians apprehensive of free trade. International trade statistics show all the benefits Canada reaped because of the free trade agreement. Let me make clear to the opposition that fear tactics will not work any more because Canadians realize, with the success of free trade, that the country's future depends on self-confidence rather than on building walls.
Naturally, building a country and being successful cannot be achieved without work. Maintaining our competitiveness is a constant struggle that will require concerted efforts from all branches of industry. That is how it works, and that is how a country and an industry can forge ahead.
One of the main factors to ensure competition and thus to secure a country's competitive position internationally is in fact the protection of intellectual property. By intellectual property, I mean patents, copyrights, trademarks, engineering drawings, integrated circuit to-
May 27, 1993

pographies, trade secrets and crop variety rights, which apply to seeds for sowing.
I think we must concentrate on this particular subject when debating NAFTA. I am happy to see that the hon. member from Frontenac is in the House, because he is an expert on copyrights and he did much to help Canadian authors when he was Minister of Communications.
Intellectual property includes innovation, in other words, ideas which, day after day, become more and more important for a country's economic development.
A country's economic development depends on information and knowledge as much as on the production of consumer goods, which means that the production of goods and services will improve.
Intellectual property, which happens to be the source of information and knowledge, has to be protected in agreements governing international trade. Canada cannot progress as a country without the protection of intellectual property. This sector is critical to the prosperity of our country. Canadian industries are calling for a more effective system for the protection of intellectual property, especially in the high technology field.
The legislation before us is particularly important because of the greater protection it gives authors and other copyright holders through amendments to the Copyright Act. Let me give a few examples of the increased protection against pirating and illicit reproduction that will result from these amendments: compliance with standards set out in the Berne Convention as revised in Paris in 1971; rental rights for copyright holders with regards to computer programs, and God knows that computer programs are an important part of that high technology field which is progressing from day to day; rental rights for copyright holders with regard to sound recordings; important measures at the borders aimed at preventing the importation of works of all kinds that are protected by copyright and have been pirated outside the country.
Compliance with the 1971 standards set out in the Berne Convention depends on various amendments made to the Copyright Act, increasing protection to
Government Orders
authors and other copyright holders. As an example, let me remind you again of the cancellation of compulsory licensing provided for in section 8 of the Copyright Act, the minor extension of the protection for non-dramatic films and videos and the explicit protection for photographs derived from negatives or otherwise.
While negotiating this North American deal, Canada and the United States managed to make Mexico aware of their concerns regarding intellectual property. They did well, as can be seen in Bill C-115 and other initiatives. We, as a nation, want to embark on negotiations with other countries, including Mexico. Mexico is undergoing a total reform of its regulations in that area. The Mexican government has abolished restrictions on royalties, increased the protection for trade secrets and simplified the registration and approval of licensing agreements.
The Mexican Congress recently passed a new act on trademarks and another one on patents extending patent protection from 14 to 20 years, hence allowing for the same protection granted in Canada.
Mexico has established severe regulations concerning compulsory licensing as well as clear legislation regarding trade secret protection. Finally, trademarks are renewed after a 10 year period.
The North American free trade agreement resolves a serious deficiency found in the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States, by establishing clear rules and guidelines in the area of intellectual property. It contains precise standards applying to copyrights, trademarks, patents, integrated circuit topographies, trade secrets, geographical designations and industrial designs.
Moreover, NAFTA provides fair regulations governing the application of intellectual property rights both in the countries and at the borders. Under NAFTA, countries will have to take measures at the borders to prevent the importation of counterfeit goods and pirated copies of works protected by copyright.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was almost pleased with As we look at the whole issue of NAFTA, I really bring my colleague's question when she said in her remarks it down to three objectives. First, it is reaffirming our that she was in favour of free trade. However, I must existing trade relationships with the United States, admit I am very displeased with the rest of it where Second, it provides an increasing access to Mexico, which
May 27, 1993

is one of the fastest growing and most promising economies in the world. Third, it will also ensure that Canada remains an attractive place to invest in terms of attracting investments from all over the world.
In my own province of British Columbia, if I could just speak about that for one moment, certainly the opportunities are almost endless when we look at the forest industry, new machinery, opportunities for western Canada's oil and gas production and opportunities for the agricultural section.
Indeed, in my role as Minister of Western Economic Diversification in recent times I have been involved in a number of trade missions to Mexico. I had the opportunity of going there at Easter and I was just amazed at the interest the Mexican buyers had in so many of our western Canadian agricultural and consumer products. There is a tremendous sense of warmth and interest in Canada and how they want to build these business alliances. They are so excited about the kinds of opportunities we have between the two countries.
Indeed, one of the things we are doing in the department is holding seminars and workshops for business people throughout the west so that they will have an opportunity to become fully aware of the kinds of opportunities there are in the Mexican market.
That brings me to another point which I think is important. One of those opportunities is in fact in the environment in environment technology and environment industries. When I was in Mexico I attended an ECOED conference again where we shared information about environmental education. They were so pleased to see the kind of leadership role that we played here in Canada on environment issues and how we could assist them in some of the challenges that they face.
Really it is in that context. It is in my role as Minister of State of Environment that I wanted to make a few remarks today because I see the NAFTA really being a milestone. In fact, it is being looked to around the world as the first trade agreement to really focus on the environment and to show the real linkages between trade and environment and sustainable development. After all, that is the objective that we all share.
It is a concept that is still somewhat new. I find as I travel that some people have some difficulty with what it is. While there may be many definitions of sustainable
Government Orders
development, the essence of the concept is that high levels of environmental quality and economic growth are complementary. They are reinforcing. A clean environment and a productive resource base are both necessary for a healthy economy and a strong economy is needed to ensure and support high social and environmental standards. It is a continuum. It is the challenge to make sure the balance is there and that continuum proceeds.
The relationship between trade and the environment is therefore essentially about sustainable development. Trade leads to economic growth which provides resources for environmental protection, while a healthy environment provides the ecological and natural resources necessary to underpin long-run economic growth stimulated by trade.
Just as a prosperous economy and a healthy environment are fully compatible, it follows that trade and the environment can also be mutually reinforcing.
The NAFTA represents the first time that environmental considerations have really been integrated into a trade agreement. We are now hearing of that in terms of the GATT, the greening of the GATT. This is also something that has to be taken into consideration as we become involved in other kinds of trade agreements as well.
For Canada it is a concrete example of trade negotiations undertaken from a sustainable development perspective. As we became involved in these discussions about NAFTA, we had a four-pronged strategy to ensure the integration of environmental considerations in the NAFTA. First of all the three countries committed in the NAFTA to implement the agreement in a manner consistent with environmental protection and to promote sustainable development. There are specific provisions throughout the agreement that build on these commitments.
First and foremost the agreement affirms the right of each country to choose the level of environmental protection that it considers appropriate. Canadians fully understand that it is important we say what we think are the appropriate standards that are necessary for Canada, how we are going to manage our scarce and valuable resources. We want to maintain that right, that sovereignty, to make those decisions.

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
As well, the trade obligations under the NAFTA specify that international environmental agreements will take precedence over the NAFTA provisions. We are involved in a wide range of agreements, whether it is the climate change convention, the biodiversity convention. We recognize there are many of these international agreements and that they are in effect supreme over the NAFTA provisions. This will also ensure as well that NAFTA will not diminish a country's right to take action under these environmental agreements.
The agreement further provides that none of the members of NAFTA-at the moment of course three potentials with others to accede to the agreement-should lower its environmental standards for the purpose of attracting investment. That is very critical and is a concern that I have heard talked about. It is the first time that a trade agreement has contained such a far-reaching commitment, a commitment made on the part of all the members.
The second prong of our strategy, which was consistent with our commitment to environmental assessment, is that the NAFTA underwent an environmental review. It was the first trade agreement to include such a review. That review ensured the ongoing and thorough consideration of environmental concerns throughout the NAFTA negotiations. It was a multi-disciplinary, interdepartmental review. The committee that was established worked with the negotiators and with environmental representatives on an ongoing basis. In keeping with the government's commitment to transparency and accountability, the full environmental review was released to the public last fall and has provided the basis for an open and informed debate on this issue.
The third prong was that there was an extensive stakeholder consultation process established for NAFTA which provided input both for the NAFTA negotiations and the environmental review. Again for the first time in the policy-making history of Canada, these groundbreaking steps have been taken. The environmental community itself has had direct input into the negotiation of a trade agreement alongside business, industry, labour and other interests.
Fourth, we recognized that we needed to do other things as well. We enhanced our existing co-operation with Mexico on environmental issues. We signed an agreement on environmental co-operation. When I was there just a few months ago we reaffirmed that agreement for a second year. Under that agreement we have initiated a wide range of projects addressing compliance, monitoring and assisting Mexico in order to deal with environmental challenges.
I know my time is limited, but I wanted to get into a discussion of some other issues. Certainly the establishment of the NACE as proposed in the discussions on a side agreement on the environment are very important, not only from the point of view of the relationship to trade but as a fundamental, important consideration recognizing that our three countries share a continent and we share the same environment. The NACE can really be a very important mechanism toward achieving sustainable development on a continental basis.
We see the NACE in a variety of roles, of being able to provide information and in ensuring sustained and longterm, effective environmental co-operation on a variety of areas. While the negotiations are not concluded, and there are some differences of opinion, we certainly are optimistic that we will be able to conclude these in a way that will meet the needs of all three countries.
A NACE focusing on technical assistance and co-operation, with provision for consultation and mediation, which we believe is a very important process in the event of a dispute resolution, would offer a tremendous forum for the achievement of sustainable development in a North American context. I see that as a real model, not only for North America but for the world to follow in implementing the vision of sustainable development put forward at Rio.
So the NAFTA has not only advantages in terms of trade, in terms of business opportunities and in terms of investment, it also, as I see it, is a tremendous opportunity to make a leap forward in our commitments and of the implementation of our goals for sustainable development as well.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the final occasion on which the House of Commons can debate the North American free trade agreement. The government has forced through the necessary measures to terminate such debate later this afternoon.
It is intent upon doing so despite the fact that only the most limited review of this important legislation and its many implications has been made.
The government's intention to curtail discussion became evident several months ago when it rejected the official opposition's repeated proposals for additional public hearings and consultations to take place across Canada that would have ensured that hearings were held in every province and territory. Proposals to hold hearings in Montreal and Toronto were rejected. Proposals to hold hearings in cities such as Hamilton and Edmonton
were rejected. Opportunities to hear more witnesses in Ottawa were rejected.
The result is that through the government's action in imposing time allocation on the debate of the North American free trade agreement, the government is denying the people of Canada and their Parliament the opportunity to fully consider the impact and ramifications of a far-reaching international agreement.
All that would be a sad spectacle in itself but it is rendered worse by the government's decision to push through this legislation without awaiting either the negotiation of the proposed side agreements or the conclusion of the NAFTA debate itself if it ever does reach a conclusion in the United States and Mexico.
By predicating his acceptance of the NAFTA on tough environmental and labour side deals President Clinton has unleashed high and perhaps insatiable expectations in the United States among those for whom North American free trade was and still is largely anathema.
Just as there is probably no negotiable side deal on labour standards which can satisfy important factions among the labour unions in the United States so too it is unlikely that all U.S. environmentalists will support an eventual trilateral environmental accord. Yet the views of the environmentalists at least will determine many votes if and when the NAFTA implementing legislation is finally brought before the United States Congress.
The need to negotiate the two side deals has delayed the introduction of the NAFTA legislation to the U.S. Congress to the point where the U.S. administration will be hard pressed to present and obtain approval for an implementing bill in time for the agreement to enter into force on January 1, 1994.
As recently as yesterday the United States trade representative raised serious doubts about the administration's ability to implement the NAFTA by January 1994 given the current differences among the three countries over the enforcement of environmental and labour side deals.
The result is that the Conservative government now finds itself caught on the horns of a policy dilemma which is entirely of its own making.. In order to justify its repeated claims that it negotiated the best possible agreement with Mexico and the United States last autumn and that the NAFTA will remain unaffected by what it might describe as footling side deals on the environment and labour, the government has committed
May 27, 1993

itself to pushing through the implementing legislation in Canada as rapidly as possible irrespective of the growing confusion and uncertainty in the United States.
In committing Canada to the NAFTA so prematurely, the government has also surrendered any influence Canada might have exercised over the negotiation of the side deals. They grow more and more significant day by day, thus paradoxically increasing the possibility that the total NAFTA package will indeed be changed in the weeks ahead but in ways that might well run contrary to Canada's national interests.
It is of more than passing significance that while the Minister of International Trade has been vehement in his opposition to anything resembling enforceable and hence potentially protectionist side accords, he has also been careful to avoid any suggestion that Canada will walk away from the NAFTA over this issue, which would be of course a logical extension of his position.
We can only assume from this studied ambiguity that behind all the puffed up rhetoric is a basic understanding that Canada will be forced in the end to accept almost any demands that the U.S. might put forward in the time ahead, including but not necessarily limited to punitive environmental trade sanctions.
In short the situation may well arise where the United States administration will tell Canada it has completed the difficult negotiation with the U.S. Congress of the side accords. It is not about to re-open those difficult negotiations so Canada and Mexico can take it or leave it and Canada, having already passed its NAFTA legislation will have nothing at all to say about the side accords. It should be added that all of this flies in the face of what has always been Canada's traditionally pragmatic and precautionary negotiating strategy.
By delaying presentation of the Canadian implementing legislation until after the equivalent bill had been presented in the U.S. Congress, Canada in the past has been able to adjust to any surprises contained in the U.S. bill with reciprocal provisions in Canadian law.
Government Orders
These surprises could come in the form of interpretations of U.S. treaty obligations revealed in the actual legislation or in add-ons. I would remind members of the notorious Baucus-Danforth amendment to the 1988 free trade agreement designed to buy congressional votes but which harm Canadian trade interests.
It is for that reason among others that Canadian governments have habitually delayed presenting firm legislated proposals to Parliament until they have had an opportunity to review the equivalent United States legislation. In that way surprises in the U.S. bill could be mirrored or reciprocated in the Canadian legislation.
This is what happened with the FTA in 1988 and indeed it certainly happened with the previous GATT agreements but it is not happening today. The government, for reasons which like the peace of God passeth all understanding, is determined in the case of NAFTA not to await confirmation of the final terms of the side accords or how the United States will implement the agreement.
In the end what makes the government's quixotic strategy most curious and indeed most dangerous is that it exemplifies how fundamentally misguided Canada's trade priorities have become. Let us not fool ourselves. Canada first entered into the free trade negotiations with Mexico and the United States in 1990 not primarily to gain enhanced access to the Mexican market nor even to improve the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement but to protect existing Canadian interests in the U.S. market which it was thought might be threatened by what then seemed to be an inevitable free trade agreement between Mexico and the United States.
Now that such an agreement is no longer inevitable why has Canada, the country least affected by NAFTA and arguably the most advantaged by its demise, emerged as its most committed proponent? What is driving the government forward when it does not know what the eventual results will be of the U.S. initiated negotiation of two and possibly more side accords?

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
Perhaps the answer to this question lies in a fundamental decision which the government made about Canada's trade and foreign policy after 1988. By explicitly turning toward continentalism and away from multilateralism or globalism the government implicitly assumed that Canada no longer had any significant role to play in setting its trade and economic priorities. In placing all its eggs in the free trade basket, the government quietly delegated to Washington major influence over Canada's trade policy agenda.
It is hardly surprising that despite perfunctory support from the world community for the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement Canada quite rightly has been perceived as quietly turning away from the multilateral trade route. This was a much vaunted Pacific Rim initiative that has yet to go beyond the rhetorical stage.
There has been virtually no attempt, public or private, to exploit the major opportunities presented in the European community. The government has not seized on the opening up of eastern Europe as a possible trade option for Canada and more importantly as a back door into the European community.
As far as Latin American is concerned the government has failed to formulate let alone implement a trade strategy except in reaction to recent U.S. and Mexican initiatives. Both actively and passively the government's whole approach to trade points to a fundamental drift if not shift toward continentalism and away from multilateralism.
It is still less than clear whether this government views NAFTA as one step toward a global trade policy or simply as the last piece in an inward-looking continental bloc. Rising protectionist sentiments in the United States together with much higher North American content requirement in NAFTA only fuel concerns that Canada is drifting into a U.S. dominated continentalist form of protection. This is an eventuality which is hardly in Canada's interest.
As barriers to trade and investment fall, Canada must be prepared to compete with the world's best in Europe and the Pacific Rim as well as in North America or risk watching its technology and productivity slip and its living standards steadily erode.
The deteriorating competitive position of the United States together with the growing ascendancy of Europe and the Pacific raise serious doubts as to whether North America is still the bench-mark against which Canadian industry should measure itself.
Canada's growing trade deficits, the imbalances that we must correct are with our partners overseas, especially with Asia and not with the United States with whom we continue to enjoy a merchandise trade surplus.
Lastly we cannot lose sight of the fact that trade in an interdependent world is largely about investment and the United States, let alone Mexico and the rest of Latin America, is hardly flush with capital. It would scarcely be useful for Canada to be locked into a trading bloc of debtors.
The movement toward regional economic integration can be seen as part of the broader movement toward global integration. Developments in telecommunications and transport are effectively diminishing geographic boundaries and constraints thereby reducing the saliency of regions.
This is especially true with regard to trade and advanced technologies, industries and services. It is naive to expect that there will soon be a time when Canada is not highly dependent on the North American continent but it would be highly naive to ignore that the world has changed dramatically since the 1960s. Canada has far greater means at its disposal today than at any point since the First World War to break out of its continental constraints and develop relations across the Pacific and to Europe.
It is ironic that it is the United States and not Canada that has emphasized the desirability of multilateralizing NAFTA, not merely by opening the way for western hemisphere countries such as Chile but by beginning discussions with the ASEAN countries for closer economic ties between them and NAFTA.
The minister of trade last August responded to a question that Canada would welcome the accession to NAFTA of Australia and New Zealand. Unfortunately the Canadian government has not pursued that possibility, thereby lessening any early prospects for the multilateralization of NAFTA in a sort of GATT-plus arrangement.
May 27, 1993

Not only has there been a failure on the part of this government to address the ways in which NAFTA might be rendered more multilateral and comprehensive in its trade benefits but there is also a failure on the part of this government to address seriously the question of how Canada equips itself to compete in an increasingly global market.
.(1315)
In a sense the FTA and NAFTA may have accelerated what would confront Canada sooner or later and certainly following the successful conclusion of the pending Uruguay Round of the GATT. The Uruguay Round will have far-reaching implications well beyond those of the continental or even hemispheric agreements such as the FTA and NAFTA.
In Canada the answer to what some see as challenges can also be seen as opportunities if we are adept enough at improving our own competitive abilities.
By refusing to confront the need for root and branch reform to the way government services are delivered, the government has also refused to recognize the direct linkage between economic liberalization, which it has pursued on a continental basis, and the need for major domestic adjustment and reform.
As the Leader of the Opposition noted recently, trade agreements are not ends in themselves. The ultimate objective is to secure a better life for the people. That means jobs and industries with a future.
During the prolonged debates about the merits or demerits of free trade, whether about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the NAFTA or the pending but far more pervasive Uruguay Round of the GATT, there has been singularly little discussion of adjustment assistance. Yet it is adjustment assistance here at home in Canada and adjustment assistance in all its many forms that can make the inevitable dislocations engendered by freer trade more understandable and more palatable even to those who are immediately adversely affected as some always will be.
Instead, today, unlike in years past, a great many Canadians are left bewildered by freer trade. For more than four decades Canadians have been assured by their governments that as a people heavily dependent upon exports for their prosperity, the improved access to
Government Orders
foreign markets and the parallel opening of our own markets was unquestionably good for them. Indeed the successive free trade rounds of the GATT, although perhaps invisible to many, did undeniably contribute massively to Canada's post-war influence.
However, part of the reason that the Kennedy and Tokyo Rounds did so was that they were matched by a commensurate degree of adjustment assistance as government initiatives which helped business and labour adapt to new opportunities and to the new competition.
Following the precedents of the various GATT rounds the Macdonald royal commission, in recommending the negotiation of a free trade agreement with the United States, urged repeatedly that any such agreement be , matched with comprehensive adjustment assistance in the form of training and retraining, investment incentives, the elimination of interprovincial trade barriers, the assistance to small business and so forth. However, the government did not do this despite promises that it would.
It sought free trade with the United States, but it did not devise, based on its own studies of the likely impact of free trade, those sectoral, regional or other assistance programs that would have helped to lessen the inevitable dislocation and to assist Canadians to compete more effectively.
In conclusion, in a post-industrial, post-cold war world environment we need to develop here in Canada a global trade and competitiveness strategy. We have the opportunity to build the first truly global outward oriented economy in North America, not just by reaching out to Mexico, but by actively seeking freer trade agreements with our major trading partners overseas, such as Japan and the European Community. First, though, we need to get the fundamentals right at home.
In this final act of the NAFTA drama we had an opportunity to write a very different conclusion from the one which we were left with in 1988. One can only regret that the government missed such an opportunity.

I find it hard to understand why anyone in Canada would be against freer trade. We have people in the NDP basically saying that we should do everything through the GATT. Canadians earn 25 per cent of their income from trade. This is more than 2.5 times the comparable figure for the U.S. and twice that of Japan. We always think of Japan as being one of the largest trading nations on a per capita basis, on a gross domestic product basis, than any country in the world. We exceed Japan.
Among the Group of Seven countries, only Germany racks up a larger portion of GDP through the buying and selling of goods. We buy. We sell. We are a trading nation.
With 27 million people Canada ranks 31st in the world in population. But our economy is the eighth largest and our per capita income is the second highest of all the industrialized countries.
One of the reasons for this has been our outstanding trade performance. Without trade we wither. Without trade we cannot survive. People should recognize that. There is the size of the population. We have the resources. We have the knowledge. We have the education. We have all of those things that go into making us a very competitive trading nation.

If we stood aside and allowed the United States and Mexico to enter into a free trade agreement it would be detrimental to Canada and to Canada's interest. If we stood aside and allowed a free trade agreement to be negotiated without our participation with the United States and Mexico, the United States would be the only country to have free access to all three markets.
What would that do? If I were an investor coming in from Japan, Korea, Singapore, Germany, France, the European Common Market or anywhere to do business and investing, I would go to the United States if Canada was not part of NAFTA. That would give me access to all three markets.

Even more serious is the human rights situation in Mexico. Here is a report from Amnesty International: "Torture with impugnity". Here is a report from the UN: "Cruel degrading punishment and anti trade union activity". Here is a report from the Inter-church Committee: "Electoral fraud and political violence".
If journalists are critical of the government in Canada they may find themselves in its doghouse but in Mexico they may find themselves in the cemetery. Even a cardinal is not safe from drug cartels.
Is it any wonder then why we in the NDP ask why this government is rushing headlong into a deal with Mexico long before long promised human rights reforms have become a reality? Why not wait and get those human rights reforms?

Millions of Canadians from coast to coast, both English and French, respect and admire Don Cherry for his deeply held passionate love for our home game and our great nation.
His tongue in cheek style along with his unique insights and witticisms are eagerly anticipated in living-rooms across the land. If some individuals choose to ascribe the blackest of connotations to Mr. Cherry's

May 27, 1993
comments on Coach's Comer then it is a sad commentary on them not on Don Cherry.
I am sure members on both sides of the House and Canadians everywhere join me in recognizing Don Cherry for who he is, a great Canadian. Let us join Don tonight to show our support as he tells it like it is from the great western forum in Los Angeles.

Madam Speaker, it may surprise some members, let alone leadership candidates, that the power given to a national leader to sign the nomination papers of a candidate was put into the Elections Act in 1974 solely for the purpose of financial accountability since candidates were given the power to issue tax receipts.
National Revenue needed to know who the legal candidate of a party was since there was a past practice of deliberately nominating candidates with the same surname to confuse the voter.
Unfortunately in the election campaign of 1974 Robert Stanfield first perverted the purpose of the power when he refused to sign the nomination papers of the mayor of Moncton because of his views on bilingualism and yet signed the nomination papers of 17 members, including Mr. Diefenbaker, who voted against the Official Languages Act.
This same ironic contradiction seems to apply to a former Minister of Justice, the current defence minister, who while professing belief in criminal reform and rehabilitation of criminals, let alone extending the right to vote to inmates in prisons, appears ready to deny her nomination signature, if she wins the leadership convention, to a candidate who may have sinned in the past but has paid his dues.
Let the people decide on a candidate and not have the divine-

Madam Speaker, I rise to applaud the appointment of Saskatchewan's Len Gustafson to the Senate.
Mr. Gustafson, with a lifetime in agriculture and 14 years of parliamentary experience, will bring to the Senate a much needed experienced voice in support of prairie agriculture.
Furthermore he will pursue his vision of international food distribution which he calls "Food a Priority". "Food a Priority" calls on the G-7 to lead a global war against starvation. The have nations would purchase food from their own farmers instead of dumping it on world markets at subsidized prices. The surplus stocks would then be given to starving people through a world-wide distribution system.
I am sure Saskatchewan people will join with me in congratulating Mr. Gustafson and wishing him well in pursuit of his dream of a world food bank.

We have listened for the last day and a half to Liberal speaker after Liberal speaker talk about how they would like to reclaim for Canada the same provisions in the NAFTA as Mexico has with respect to energy.

Where does the duplicity end? Where?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some time ago I received a letter from Philip Carpenter, at the time a grade four student from Truro, Nova Scotia. He was requesting that the Canadian government require that all oil tankers operating in Canadian waters be equipped with double hulls in order to prevent environmental damage as a result of oil spills.
I am pleased to tell Philip that Canada has recently adopted tough new standards which will require that all new tankers ordered after July 6, 1993 be built with double hulls. These regulations apply to all new tankers and are some of the most strict in the world.
Also, as of July 6, 1995 most existing single hull crude tankers will be required to be phased out when they reach the age of about 25 or 30 years.
I am not sure if Philip's letter alone resulted in these changes or not, but I do congratulate Philip and all those young people who take a keen interest in environmental issues and take the time to write us.
I also want to congratulate the Coast Guard and the Minister of the Environment and his officials for their action in this effort.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on a matter that is very important to me as a member of Parliament and to many Canadians who fought for freedom during World War II.
Let us take note of the fact that a Canadian delegation is today in Liverpool, England, joining the British in their commemoration of the Battle of the Atlantic. While our official commemoration took place a couple of weeks ago we should again pause to salute those brave soldiers, seamen and RCAF veterans who provided such valiant service during World War II. It was their commitment, their dedication and their lives which helped turn the tide during World War II.
The longest battle during the war seems so long ago, however it is like yesterday to those who participated.
My commitment as Official Opposition critic for veterans affairs is to ensure all veterans, those who have sacrificed so much for us to live freely today, are not forgotten by Canadians.
I urge this House to make a commitment to the veterans of Canada to ensure that they are taken care of as they grow old gracefully.

Madam Speaker, during the spring and winter of 1992 a special joint committee of this House and the Senate held a number of meetings to determine the way conflict of interest legislation involving members of Parliament ought to be handled.
The committee totally rejected Bill C-43 on the Order Paper and recommended a bill involving the appointment of a jurisconsult and full disclosure of assets of members of Parliament as the best method of disciplining issues involving conflict.
The government has rejected the unanimous committee report in Bill C-116 by again insisting on the

May 27, 1993
Oral Questions
concepts of Bill C-43 that are contained in that bill. It is unfortunate the government cannot accept the unanimous report filed with this Elouse which was made by 21 members of Parliament.

Madam Speaker, Canadians will recall that when the whole debate over the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was raging five years ago the one certainty which most boosters of the deal shared was that Alberta was surely going to be a big winner.
The reports are in, the facts have been tallied and the results are clear. Alberta, too, has lost under free trade. From December 1988 to December 1992 Albertans have lost a net total of almost 13,000 jobs. When one factors out oil and gas sales to the U.S., sales which were already deregulated and have nothing to do with the free trade agreement, we find that the dollar value of Alberta exports to the U.S. failed to even keep up with inflation. Therefore, like the rest of Canada, Alberta and Albertans have lost under free trade and no amount of happy talk can change that.
It is time to scrap the original free trade deal and ditch the North American free trade agreement.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last year on December 11 I rose in the House to ask the Prime Minister not to make dozens of patronage appointments in the dying days of his mandate. Since that day, there have been 526 Order in Council appointments.
May 27, 1993

Everybody remembers in 1984 when the Prime Minister said in attacking the then Prime Minister, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra: "It will never, never happen under a Conservative government".
Today I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he would have the courtesy to apologize to the people of Canada, and in particular, to the former leader of my party, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that the former leader of the Liberal Party would think that if anyone owes him an apology, it is the present leader of the Liberal Party.
May I first indicate that the number used by my hon. friend is typically misleading. He holds up a document saying to table the document right away, then the media can see that this document relates to Order in Council appointments which cover public servants, government agencies and commissions which deal with non-political people. The number is used to mislead and to try to mislead the press into thinking that any government in Canadian history could ever replicate the orgy of appointments made by the Liberal government of which he was a member in 1984.
My hon. friend asked about appointments to the Senate. In Meech Lake we sought to share the power of appointment to the Senate with the provinces and this was rejected. In Charlottetown we sought to have the members of the Senate elected by the people and this was rejected. The parliamentary system continues to function until there are further changes.
Therefore, we have made some appointments, for example, Jean-Claude Rivest, Mr. Bourassa's chief of staff and former adviser and the former member for Saint-Denis, the Liberal dean of the House. Madam Speaker, I am having difficulty trying to respond.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We may be able to continue on a supplementary question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quoting the words of the Prime Minister in 1984. At that time the Senate was operating like it is today. To use the excuse that he offered to make some changes to the Senate does not excuse what he is trying to do today. Not only did he name senators but he
Oral Questions
also forced other senators to retire before the end of their mandate so that he could make new appointments. We know of other instances where people have resigned their mandates of three years so they will be able to gain a seven-year appointment. That is a fraud.
I want to know whether the Prime Minister remembers when he said in 1984: "I think that what has taken place is completely unacceptable in an open and democratic society".
Will the Prime Minister tell me why it was unacceptable in 1984 but is so justifiable in 1993?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, the statement that I had forced senators to retire is of course false. I would ask the Leader of the Opposition to withdraw that.
Second, my friend asks why what took place and was unacceptable in 1984 is acceptable today. Well, it was unacceptable in 1984 because an outgoing Prime Minister refused to make the appointments himself and he passed the appointments over to an unelected Prime Minister who was not a member of this House and had never sought nor obtained the confidence of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, here is a new theory now: the Prime Minister is no longer the Prime Minister.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am trying to understand the Hon. Leader of the Opposition while waiting for this House to quiet down. The Hon. Leader of the Opposition has the floor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister at the time was right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra who had the privilege which the Prime Minister has today, but the Prime Minister used it to win the election. I would like to ask the Prime Minister the following question: Yesterday, the Minister of the Environment said that the Prime Minister should no longer make such appointments, and it was reported in the newspaper this morning by Michel Vastel.
Were you there?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, no, I was not there. But will the Prime Minister heed the advice of his environment minister, who says that it is enough and that he should

May 27, 1993
Oral Questions
not continue to make such appointments now, when he himself said in 1984 that it was immoral to do so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Three questions, three preambles, three completely erroneous statements which the Leader of the Opposition ought to retract.
He says anything at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Yes, he says anything at all to convince the media. I was asked what the difference was. The difference is that we have a duly elected government, whether the member likes it or not. The Prime Minister is exercising his responsibilities, whereas in 1984 the outgoing Prime Minister refused to make appointments, but insisted that his successor make about 40 appointments although this successor had not been elected either to Parliament or as Prime Minister.
I point out to my friend what the Montreal Gazette said on December 18, 1992:

"Prime Minister Mulroney was simply recognizing a basic fact this week when he gave notice that he will return to the old system of appointing members of the upper house of Parliament. Mr. Mulroney cannot act as though the referendum had no force. He has to respect the decision of the people," and under the Constitution that requires the appointment pursuant to those criteria.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You had an option.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: My hon. friend says I had an option. Yes, indeed. And he has an option. For example, if we are going to get the NAFTA legislation through the Senate, if he will give me the assurance that he will support it here and instruct his senators in the other place to support it, I will give him the undertaking that we will not make any more Senate appointments.
Madam Speaker, it may come as a novel idea for the Prime Minister but we in this party do not trade patronage for principle.
Oh, oh.

We are not prepared to sell out the country to avoid a few more Tories in the Senate by Brian Mulroney.
Since December this Prime Minister has made 526 Order in Council appointments, over 100 appointments a month. As this Prime Minister feels the reins of power slipping from his fingers and as they cling on for a last few days, Canadians want to know whether or not he will come to his senses and end his orgy of patronage, his manna from heaven for Tories, his privileged position to the chosen few who are not enemies of Canada and put an end to the Tory patronage now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Brian, if you keep this up, you are going to give hypocrisy a bad name.
My hon. friend says that we made 526 appointments since December, 100 a month. How does he explain former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau making 225 appointments in one week?
Madam Speaker, we have the answer. My hon. friend from Halifax just said that the Liberals were more efficient. I will concede that the Liberals could not organize and run a two-car funeral but in terms of patronage, they were more efficient than any other government in the history of Canada.
Madam Speaker, when it comes to Brians and hypocrisy that Brian takes the cake.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us all be careful that what is said in jest does not become insults on both sides of the House.

Madam Speaker, I apologize. It is not a laughing matter; it is quite serious. We would not want to mislead the Speaker or anybody else in the House.
In today's Le Droit Michel Vastel quotes the Minister of the Environment as noting that the current Senate as constituted after yesterday's appointments sees 47 sitting Conservative members and 41 sitting Liberal members. He has noted that with those numbers the Prime Minister's concern about legislation being passed is not a concern, that the Conservatives control the current Senate. Then the Minister of the Environment went on to say that these appointments were enough for the moment.
May 27, 1993

Is the Prime Minister prepared to consider, if not the words of New Democrats, Liberals or civic minded citizens, the advice of the Minister of the Environment who said enough is enough?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just for the record, the Minister of the Environment said no such thing. My hon. friend just said the Minister of the Environment said enough is enough. That is a false statement. The Minister of the Environment said no such thing. The abuse of the truth by the Leader of the Opposition and the member from Newfoundland today is not a surprise.
I will reflect upon what my hon. friend said.
Do you want to read what he said?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: It is okay, Brian. I will reflect upon what you said if you will undertake to reflect upon this: "When you take one member of Parliament from the House of Commons to the Senate do you realize you save money? If I appoint you to the Senate I pay you full pay. If I appoint an MP I pay his full pay but he doesn't draw a pension. I am in favour of these appointments". Jean Chretien, August 1, 1984.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, what is needed here as we listen to the squabble between these two parties is a simple plan, and I would like to propose one: let's abolish the Senate.
Abolish it, abolish it.

Madam Speaker, while the debate about those who are employed is very interesting, the debate about the two million Canadians who are unemployed should be the real concern of this House.
My question is for the Prime Minister. As he knows over half of Canada's manufacturing industry is owned by foreign investors, mostly Americans. Seventy-seven per cent of our trade already goes to the United States and more than 15 per cent of our natural resources are foreign owned. Apparently the Prime Minister is not satisfied with this amount of foreign ownership. He wants to ram NAFTA through the House to make sure that we give over the rest.
Oral Questions
I want to ask the Prime Minister a serious question. Is he really satisfied to retire as the first Prime Minister of Canada to give away Canada's sovereignty rather than to build it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just by way of a prefatory remark I would draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that I proposed the abolition of the Senate on the floor of the House of Commons in 1985. We sought to move it along and indeed, as she knows, in both Meech and in Charlottetown we proposed the abolition of the Senate as it presently is and its reconstitution as an elected body. I think my hon. friend is fully au courant of that.
The sovereignty of a nation is achieved and defended in large measure by its economic strength. In Canada's case our economic strength comes from trade. We are a trading nation. Almost 30 per cent of our GDP comes from international trade as opposed to a country such as the United States or Japan where that number is in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent or 15 per cent. We trade to live and trade means opening new trading opportunities such as we have with the United States in the free trade agreement and now with Mexico in NAFTA.
If my hon. friend would care to look at the numbers, our trade with the United States since the free trade agreement is up by almost 20 per cent. That is about $19 billion and for every billion dollars there is some very significant job creation; 15,000 new jobs have been created. This country will achieve new prosperity and greater sovereignty by enhancing its wealth and we do that by greater trade.

Madam Speaker, this country will only achieve success when Canadians are working. With an unemployment at 11.7 per cent it is clear these trade arrangements have been disastrous for Canada, for Canadian workers and for Canadians jobs.
I say to the Prime Minister that we were very pleased yesterday to co-sponsor an amendment to the NAFTA bill with a former member of his cabinet, a current Tory member, to point out the absurdity of trying to implement NAFTA at a time of high unemployment.

May 27, 1993
Oral Questions
If the Prime Minister is not willing to listen to Canadians, if he is not willing to listen to real alternatives, would he listen to some of his own caucus members and stop NAFTA now? Let's not have the implementation of NAFTA.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course I would be happy to listen to any reasonable alternatives. I have no quarrel at all with that. In fact the object of the exercise in the House of Commons is precisely to listen to and learn new and better ideas.
My hon. friend says that the trade deal has been a disaster. She may be right, but perhaps she could consider the following facts. Canada exported $19.6 billion more to the United States in 1992 than it did in 1988. In March 1993 our exports to the United States were 21 per cent ahead of their level in March 1992. Canada's trade surplus with the United States reached $17.7 billion in 1992, the highest level since 1985.
This is the most powerful and dynamic trading relationship that exists anywhere in the world between two sovereign nations. Clearly the free trade agreement has enhanced that. I would think my hon. friend would find it in her interest and that of her colleagues to support a free trade agreement which extends benefits to Mexico and then to other countries in Latin America.

Madam Speaker, there is one important statistic the Prime Minister refuses to address, and that is the unemployment statistic where we have one in four people either looking for a job or underemployed.

I have another question for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister refuses to understand. Unemployment in our country is over 11 per cent. This is a tragedy for Canadians. It makes no sense to conclude trade agreements that will cause even more unemployment. Why is the Prime Minister in such a hurry to pass his bill? There is no reason now. The bill has not been tabled in the United States Congress.
My question for the Prime Minister is therefore this: Why is the government in such a hurry? What did his government promise the United States, international financiers and multinationals? What are the agreements or understandings with the United States? Who required that this bill pass now? Why not wait for the election?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is essentially the same question I was asked yesterday, about waiting for an election. There will be an election in the summer, fall or winter. I don't know. The member and her party will then have plenty of opportunities to put forward their positions on international trade.
For example, in a recent interview, the Hon. John Ciaccia, Quebec's Minister of International Affairs, said that to make our businesses more competitive, we have to open up new markets and protect some of our industries.
The free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico gives us this opportunity. So it is a way to create jobs, make life easier for people and increase our international trade and that is why we are for it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I responded in part to that question just two or three days ago to the hon. member's colleague from Prince George.
As my hon. friend knows this was the subject of the panel hearing. We supported the position that he has just expressed on behalf of the Government of British Columbia. We will continue to do so.
The panel itself did not rule that Canadian log export controls are a countervailable benefit. We will continue to work with the industry and the province to follow this through.
I should say that the finding only applies to log export measures that were examined in the countervailing duty investigation. It has no precedence in other investigations.

Madam Speaker, I deeply appreciate the fact that the current Minister for International Trade has publicly said he will continue to fight for the right of British Columbia to export logs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by stating loud and clear that Liberals are not against free trade. We are free traders. We recognize that Canada is a trading nation and that the United States is our largest trading partner. However the difference between us and the Conservatives is that we want fair trade. We want access to the American market. We believe that true free trade has to secure us the U.S. market which neither the FTA nor the North American free trade deal does.
In 1988 we opposed the Canada-U.S. free trade deal because it was flawed and not because we were against free trade. In 1993 we are again criticizing a flawed agreement. On the other hand, our colleagues in the NDP would have us build up walls around this country. They remain intellectually dishonest to Canadians about
May 27, 1993

Canada's changing economy and the fact that Canada is a trading nation.
I remind the NDP that one in five Canadian jobs in this country is directly dependent upon trade with other countries around the world. This is a reality and the NDP has to come to terms with that.
When the North American free trade negotiations began the Liberals felt it provided an opportunity for the Canadian government to correct the flaws of the FTA. We had hoped that some of the important issues we brought forward with these flaws would be addressed in these negotiations such as a subsidies code. Free trade cannot be free trade without defining what a subsidy is between the two countries in a trading arrangement. Canadians know that and they are having a difficult time getting their products into the United States because the Americans claim we are subsidizing.
Look at the situation with tripartite stabilization. The Americans call that a subsidy. As farmers in our communities know, it is an insurance policy for our farmers that allows them an opportunity to farm, to be able to have some sort of projected income and to be able to respond to market conditions. The free trade deal did not do anything to help these farmers and it did nothing to help get their products into the United States.
We asked for a more effective dispute resolution mechanism but this deal threw out the negotiating bodies, the boards that were set up to facilitate trade between our two countries.
We asked for agreed upon labour standards and environmental standards and foremost, as my hon. friend knows, we wanted the same energy protection as Mexico and we did not get it.
We had hoped at the very least the Government of Canada would be seeking changes this time around that would help facilitate trade between our two countries. The government has not come close to addressing any of these problems. This House cannot support in particular this trade arrangement among Canada, the United States and Mexico because it goes against the interests of Canada.
I would like to talk about the implementation of this agreement and about the fact that this government one
Government Orders
hour into the debate decided to cut it off. As soon as the debate started it cut it off. It said it had negotiations and talks across the country. The Prime Minister himself said this is one of the most critical economic issues facing this country yet this government cut off debate one hour into it.
Because a lot of Canadians do not understand this debate, they need firsthand information. They need to listen to this debate because it is important to them. It is important to their jobs for the future. It is important to their children's livelihood. Canadians want this bill debated.
The government says that our future prosperity, jobs and growth will depend on some sort of North American free trading arrangement. Yet once again it has given us a deal that is not free trade. Since the last deal came in, 300,000 manufacturing jobs have been eliminated by an agreement that supposedly gave us an open market to the United States.
We all know what happened in the dying days of the negotiations and how a political arrangement was made among the Minister for International Trade, the Prime Minister and the Americans to get a deal for an election at any cost to Canadians.
When I spoke on this same issue last September I talked about the viability of our steel industry and how it was being undermined by the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States. We have seen a situation in recent weeks in my hon. colleague's area in Hamilton. Dofasco has decided to go to the United States to build a mini-mill. It will create jobs in the United States. Why? We found out why.
It wanted to get away from Americans who were harassing it while shipping its products to the United States. It just took the jobs and shipped them over there. It built a plant over there. We in Canada, especially in the Niagara peninsula, in Haldimand-Norfolk and Hamilton lost these jobs to Americans because Dofasco did not have the access to the American market that the government claims it has.
As I said before, this deal now gets rid of the working groups. Under chapter 19 of the FTA, rules for dumping and countervailing duties were to be negotiated by the end of 1995. That is right in the deal. We said: "That's fine. At least we'll have an opportunity to find out what a

subsidy is. At least we'll have an opportunity to make sure our anti-dumping laws are the same".
What happened? The government threw all that out. It got rid of it. What did it get in return? My hon. colleague across the way asked what it got in return. What did it get in return for throwing out these working groups? Nothing. Absolutely nothing.
The fact is that this government's trade deals have not secured access to the American market. We are powerless to deflect U.S. protectionism. What did we give up? We gave up sovereignty. In a lot of cases in this area we gave up the right not only of our federal government but of our provincial governments to have a say in their own affairs.
Look at energy and the national provisions. We now have to give national treatment to the Americans, even in an energy crisis.
What does that mean for Canadians? As an example let us look at Montreal in Quebec where there is Hydro Quebec. Around the Montreal area many companies have started up because Quebec has been able to give special treatment to corporations with cheap power.
Now under national treatment rules Quebec will not be able to do that. American companies could set up shop in upstate New York, Vermont, northern New Hampshire or the northern states and they will have to be sold the power at the same price as a company in Canada. What benefit is that to Canadians? What did Canada get in return for giving that up?
I want to conclude by saying that while I believe that trade deals are important to a trading nation like Canada, we must not lose sight of what is in the best interests of Canadians. The lack of a subsidies code hurts Canadian workers.
I want to stress that Canadians can compete. We can compete with anyone in the world. Our Canadian farmers, the farmers in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk, can compete with anybody. They can compete with the Americans as long as they have a level playing field on which to compete.
What this does to supply management is just terrible. The government is going across this country telling farmers that supply management is protected under this
deal. That is completely false because to have supply management two specific main factors have to be there.
We have to be able to stop the product at the border and we must have quantitative restrictions, but we also must have a food processing industry that can compete and take that food, process it and sell it.
This sends it south of the border. Over the last four years we have lost over 100 food processing industries in this country and this NAFTA deal just extends that. It opens the borders to these industries going across the border.
With the stalemate at the GATT we cannot count on the GATT agreement to resolve this problem of subsidies and anti-dumping. That is why I find it so frustrating that this government has given up this opportunity in this debate to resolve some of these critical issues affecting trade in this country.

What is it really all about? Very simply tariffs will be reduced between Mexico and Canada over the 10-year period. It is very similar to that enjoyed by the FTA. Of course Mexican licensing requirements will also be removed over the 10-year period. It is a very important point particularly as far as the auto industry is concerned.

That certainly is what the auto parts manufacturers in my area of Guelph-Wellington wanted. They wanted us to move higher. Of course we had debates on whether it should be 50 or 75, and people finally settled I think appropriately at 62.5 per cent.
Services are very important to Canada. We have available tremendous engineering, accounting, legal, business and professional services of all kinds. It has been very difficult for us to sell those services in Mexico. Now we can do it. Under the North American free trade agreement Canadian business people, particularly those in the high-tech end, will be able to go to Mexico to sell the products we have in Canada and the services that Canada can provide. Obviously basic telecommunications are left out of this agreement as they were left out of the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to briefly address what I consider to be the most important economic horizon in the pursuit of Canadian prosperity and that is our future potential for world trade.
It is a fact that Canada has always been, and now more than ever continues to be, a trading nation. To an extent more than most Canadians realize, our high standard of living and our enviable social programs are based on the economic foundation which we have established as a world trader. More than 25 per cent of our national income is generated by trade, which is a proportion that is at least twice as large as the comparable trade content in the economies of countries such as the U.S.A. and Japan.
During the 1980s for example Canadian exports grew at an average annual rate of more than 5 per cent in real terms. It was a full 2 percentage points faster than our economy grew as a whole. It is evidence of just how much Canadians do and must continue to rely on trade to maintain and increase our economic prosperity. We have no alternative but to constantly seek out and develop world-wide markets for our goods and services. It is absolutely essential, both to the solution of our immedi-

May 27, 1993
Government Orders
ate economic problems and to the sustenance of lasting future prosperity, that Canada pursues an active trade policy and aggressively advances our competitive participation in trade with all comers of the world.
What truly stands out about Canada in world economic comparisons is the disproportionate success which we enjoy economically among all nations, which is an achievement that has essentially been created by our outstanding trade performance. With only 27 million people Canada ranks thirty-first in population size, yet our economy is the eighth largest in the world. More important, our per capita income is the second highest of all industrialized nations.
In terms of trade Canada has been a David among the Goliaths of the world. That is the unique economic strategy that we must continue to employ in the future. That is to seek trading opportunities in markets of the world that are far beyond our size and yet in which we are prepared to compete and able to compete freely. Nothing exemplifies this strategy more than does the free trade agreement with the United States where we have accepted the risks of competing with a country 10 times our size because we believe that the market opportunity is so disproportionately in our favour.
With the proposed expansion of the FTA to include Mexico under a new North American free trade agreement, we are pursuing that strategy further to create a total trading bloc of 360 million people of which Canada will be less than 8 per cent in population size, but a vastly larger proportion in terms of our share of the economic potential.
Simply put, the strategic trading opportunities offered by the comparative markets of Canada, the United States and Mexico are almost 13 to 1 in Canada's favour.
As we know, I am a member of Parliament from the Atlantic region. Nowhere in Canada is trade more crucial to the economy than in our part of the country. Our people and our economies in all of the Atlantic provinces have benefited significantly from increased exports to the United States under the free trade agreement.
It is important to note that over half of our exports from that region go to the United States alone. Some of the 1992 figures are worthy of note.
My own province of New Brunswick sold $1.9 billion to the United States last year, two-thirds of our total exports. These figures include pulp and paper, mineral fuels, food products, engineering services and a host of related products.
For Nova Scotia total sales to the United States in 1992 were $1.6 billion, again more than two-thirds of total exports from that province. They included fish, rubber products, iron and steel, pulp and paper, and so on. Even for small Prince Edward Island, the United States market purchased $100 million worth of goods and services especially in fish and food products. The Newfoundland total was over $600 million, also heavily based on fish, paper and mineral fuels.
These are impressive figures for an area the size of Atlantic Canada, totalling more than $4.2 billion and representing a very significant portion of our total exports.
There can be no doubt that the free trade agreement has had a major beneficial impact on these current sales. However its greatest potential still lies before us.
This is even more true when Mexico is included because current trade between Atlantic Canada and Mexico is very small, representing less than 2 per cent of the total. Thus the prospects for growth in a new free trading relationship with that country are entirely on the up side. Many significant opportunities have already been identified.
Although both Atlantic Canada and Mexico are reliant on resource industries such as forestry, mining, agriculture and fishing, there are differences in the types of commodities, the growing seasons and the markets which would tend to limit to any significant extent direct competition.
With new and more open access to the Mexican market of 85 million people, one that is experiencing rapid economic reform and expansion, Atlantic Canada businesses should be able to dramatically increase their sales penetration there.
May 27, 1993

Once NAFTA is finalized the removal of trade barriers and the clarification of trading rules will make it easier for Atlantic companies to do business in that market.
For example, with respect to fish products the removal of tariffs and import licence requirements will permit companies like Connors Brothers from New Brunswick to significantly increase participation in a market that has a total potential of $1.4 billion.
The Mexican chemical market is expected to grow by as much as 30 per cent over the next five years. Companies such as Diagnostic Chemicals Limited of Prince Edward Island have already commenced selling their products through a distribution alliance in Mexico.
In forest products Mexico imports almost $1 billion annually. This demand is expected to grow at the rate of 12 per cent annually over the next five years. This means major opportunities for several forest products companies in Atlantic Canada.
Mexico imports almost $2 billion worth of ferrous and non-ferrous metals each year. Its import requirements of steel and metal are expected to increase 14 per cent annually over the next five years. Sydney Steel already makes steel rails for that market.
The demand in Mexico for agricultural food products is expected to grow by more than 30 per cent each year. There will be significant opportunities for companies such as McCain's and Ganong Brothers and Clearwater Fine Foods of Nova Scotia to participate in that market.
The highly publicized environmental problems in Mexico offer distinct opportunities for engineering and manufacturing firms that specialize in pollution treatment and environmental engineering.
Companies such as ADI Limited, Neill and Gunter, Jacques Whitford, Nolan Davis, Crandall Engineering and others are all looking seriously at Mexico as a market of opportunity. Many of them already have established relationships there.
I want to digress for a moment to talk about a recognition that has been accorded to one of those firms symbolic and representative of them all. In 1992 World-business for the second year recognized ADI Limited as one of the world's great innovative engineering companies, particularly with respect to its export reputation. I quote:

"The company maintains its outstanding reputation for engineering work within Canada while continuing to establish impressive credentials from the U.S.A. to eastern Europe. Also to its credit, the company is diversifying into related activities in which it and New Brunswick possess world-class capabilities.
This is an example of a relatively small company with an outstanding reputation for quality work headquartered in one of Canada's smallest provinces making a very significant contribution to Canadian export activities".
That company is now active in Mexico. The Worldbusi-ness magazine award goes on to indicate that New Brunswick was acknowledged as demonstrating the strongest international business orientation of any province in Canada in 1992.
I see my time is running out. I can only say it is clear that the free trade agreement with the United States has been good for Canada and it has been good for Atlantic Canada. By including Mexico in its market, which is more than three times as large as Canada's, the potential for free trade continues to be enhanced as the foundation for our country's economic future.
Beyond North America the NAFTA partners have a clear vision of expanding that trading bloc into Latin America commencing with Chile.
In all of these directions world trade will become Canada's road to prosperity and competitiveness will be the key to our success. Canada must be a country where competitive spirit is the watchword, where growth and progress are achieved because we take pride in doing things better, faster and more economically than our trading partners.
While world trade represents Canada's external potential for growth, our domestic market also must be enhanced. Our challenge is to achieve the best of all trading opportunities, those which now exist here at home, those which exist immediately throughout North America and those which will eventually emerge for us around the globe.
