speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, March 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-285, an Act to amend the Citizenship Act (oath of allegiance), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Human Resources envelope.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for introducing his private members' bill, Bill C-285, an act to amend the Citizenship Act.
In this country, what all members of this House have in common is our citizenship. Citizenship is what links millions of men and women who choose to be Canadians.

For 125 years Canadians have pledged allegiance to the British Crown. However over those years successive governments have taken steps that have helped build a unique Canadian identity. We have taken steps to ensure that while we maintain our strong links with Britain, we evolve into something truly unique.
In 1947 we began with our first Citizenship Act. We were no longer British subjects. In 1967 we saluted the Maple Leaf for the very first time as a unique Canadian symbol. In 1980 O Canada replaced God Save the Queen as our national anthem. In 1982 we patriated our Constitution from Britain.
It is time today that when new citizens of this country take the oath of citizenship they do so with just one thing in mind: Canada. I still believe that our British parliamentary heritage is fundamental to who we are as a nation and this tradition must be preserved.
I believe there is a role for the monarchy in Canadian political life as well as in Canadian legal life. The Queen
Private Members' Business
shall remain head of state, but I do not think that she or her heirs and successors have a role to play in Canada's oath of citizenship.

I feel that by debating this issue and subsequently voting in favour of this bill, we will send a very clear message to Canadians about the value we put on our citizenship. We want the federal government to promote the concept of what it means to be a Canadian citizen, so that we can be truly proud of being what we are and achieve a real understanding of what it means to be a Canadian.

I believe changing the oath of citizenship could help us build this greater sense of belonging that we have been looking for. We would be sending a very clear message to Canadians, both native bom and naturalized alike, that Canada comes first. It is important that citizens believe they can change Canadian society. People must believe they will have an impact on Canadian lives.
As I have very often said, active and equal participation is the key to citizenship. We need to encourage all Canadians to get involved and have a say in the way this country is governed. The oath of citizenship should be an inclusive statement that reflects the values we cherish as a society.
When new citizens come to this country, stand before the citizenship judge and recite the oath they should have a feeling that they will be part of a society they can mould and shape, a society for which they will have a true sense of belonging. The oath of citizenship should encourage faith in and love for Canada.
It in no way takes away from our attachment to the British part of our heritage. It builds on our self-identity and self-awareness and that is so needed at this particular time in our history.
I was reading through a magazine today. I believe it was Maclean's. It talked about Australia where for the very first time the Attorney General last month became the first ever cabinet minister to recite an oath of office that pledges allegiance to the Commonwealth of Austra-

May 27, 1993
Private Members' Business
lia. In his opinion it simply reflects national realities as Australia enters the 21st century. What are we doing about our 21st century?

Madam Speaker, the oath of allegiance for new Canadian citizens should reflect more accurately the Canadian experience. We need a new oath of allegiance, and I intend to support this bill.

Madam Speaker, the amendment before the House today proposed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace refers to only one aspect of the Canadian Citizenship Act which is a broad piece of legislation serving all Canadians. Merely changing the oath of ' citizenship which has far-reaching implications for many Canadians is really a piecemeal approach to legislation that should be dealt with in its entirety.
The issue of the Canadian Citizenship Act is not dormant. The government is examining the act presently and the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship, my colleague the hon. member for Pierrefonds-Dollard, has held consultations with citizens and groups all across Canada on how to improve that act. This will lead to a thorough reassessment of the current act and eventually to a new act.
Consultations also have been held between members of the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and other departments that have a common interest in the Canadian Citizenship Act such as the Solicitor General and Employment and Immigration.
The new Canadian Citizenship Act should apply not only to immigrants to Canada but should be a broader act applicable to every Canadian. It should address the broader concerns associated with Canadian citizenship. As I have said in this House previously, it baffles me to some degree that those of us who are native-born Canadians for the most part have never received a certificate of citizenship and to some degree envy those new Canadians who go through the citizenship process, take the citizenship oath and have a citizenship ceremony. It is something that I think all Canadians should have the privilege and the honour to participate in and enjoy. I recommended to the minister previously that some method should be found to ensure that the children of
this nation at some appropriate time in their education be given the opportunity to participate in a citizenship ceremony and to take the oath of citizenship.
Canadian citizenship including all its responsibilities is more important than just the oath of citizenship. It affirms that all the rights and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship are understood and are accepted.
If the suggested amendment is really a disguised attempt to change our constitutional monarchy form of government then it is not the appropriate approach and I am not sure that that is the intent of the amendment. The government does not wish to see such an amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act being used as a stepping stone toward that end.
Such a change would also ignore an important part of our history and our cultural heritage as Canadians. The oath of citizenship is being singled out for change. None of the other acts requiring oaths are proposed for change. The oath of citizenship is substantially the same as the oath for every member of Parliament, the same as the oath for every member of the Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is the same oath as sworn by all federal public servants.
Finally, the government gave a commitment in the House not to delete the reference to the Queen in the oath of allegiance. To accept the amendment before the House would be to renege on the assurance that the government has that it has no intention of withdrawing Her Majesty from the oath of allegiance.
The oath of citizenship is being singled out for change. As I said earlier, none of the other oaths of office have been so addressed or proposed.
The immediate impact of the change would be to make an important symbolic change. Such symbols have to be understood in their historical context and as part of our heritage.
The Crown is one such important symbol. It is part and parcel of our Canadian heritage and remains central to our constitutional monarchy. Every Canadian learns about the role of the monarch in our Constitution through the education process. Every new Canadian learns about it while going through the immigration and citizenship application process. I repeat that I think that introduction to citizenship should pertain to every student formally in their education. Every Canadian should
May 27, 1993

have the opportunity in his or her lifetime to take the oath of allegiance to receive a certificate of citizenship.
I hope that the minister will continue to consider an innovation or an initiative to the Canadian Citizenship Act that will cause that to happen. It is one of the major differences that distinguishes Canadians from Americans. Virtually every Canadian understands this in terms of our citizenship.
It is for these reasons that I am opposed to the proposed amendment to the oath of citizenship and if it comes to a vote I will vote against it.

Madam Speaker, the private members' bill before the House today was introduced by our colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace and concerns the oath of allegiance. I listened to the hon. member opposite when he gave his opinion, but I think he missed the point of this bill.
If we look at the history of our country before 1867, when we were still a British colony, at one point England decided to give its colonies responsible government. That is when we had the union of Upper and Lower Canada. This was followed by one of the world's great revolutions, and I am referring to Confederation as established by the British North America Act. That was the first step.
Obviously, the monarchy has played a very important role in our history. It is part of our history. In high school when they study history students realize that England's role was far more important than the role played by France in this country.
After Confederation, Canada took part in World War I, and even the Boer War in 1899. Canada played a major role, especially during World War I, when we lost thousands of Canadians who went over to help the British troops in Europe. In fact, Canada's involvement and sacrifices in World War I were considerable.
Subsequently, there were further developments. In 1931, the Government of Canada experienced the first loosening of its ties with Great Britain, when we had our first Department of External Affairs. It was now up to the Government of Canada to formulate its own foreign
Private Members' Business
policy. We no longer had to ask the British government what our position should be.
After 1931, there was World War II, where Canada again played a very important role with Britain and our other allies. Here again, we demonstrated our ability, sometimes at considerable cost, to overcome the threats surging on all sides. After that war, the process accelerated and citizenship came under Canadian jurisdiction. Vincent Massey became the first Canadian-born Governor General. Previously, our governor generals had come from Britain and were appointed by the monarch.
Over the years, Canada went through a number of phases. It was not because we wanted to break our ties with the monarchy. It was simply the way we evolved as a people. This country had earned its place in the world. It made sacrifices during both world wars, and it had shown its compassion by welcoming people from all over the world within its borders.
And these people helped build Canada. History tells us few countries have been as welcoming as Canada, a country where people of all races came to live. Think about it. It was a real experiment. Will it be a success? Only time will tell, because it is still too early to say that all these people came here to build one country.
As my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace pointed out in his speech, it was entirely legitimate for a country with a population of over 22 million to want its own flag. I don't think that has diminished the role or the symbol of the monarchy in this country. Not at all. But it was something that had to be done because our identity as a nation is important.
I went to a citizenship ceremony, and I admit I had never stopped to think about the oath of allegiance, because I had never been to this kind of ceremony before. I was surprised because I had assumed people swore allegiance to Canada and possibly to the Constitution. As my colleague mentioned earlier, the monarchy is mentioned in the Constitution. Personally, and I believe this applies to most Canadians I have known over the years, my allegiance is to my country, Canada, whether we are talking about our national anthem, our flag or our independence vis-a-vis other countries. The oath of allegiance is a very important step and, in my

May 27, 1993
Private Members' Business
opinion, it does not reflect our history, in other words, that we used to have a monarchy.
This is just a normal part of the process for a nation worthy of the name, with its own symbols, a nation that has welcomed people coming from every country on this planet. It stands to reason that these people should swear an oath of allegiance to their new country, Canada. Since they are here, they will abide by the laws of the land and, like all Canadians, they will abide by the Constitution of our country, the basis of our rights and freedoms.
It would be ridiculous to see this as a part of a conspiracy to get rid of the monarchy in this country. The monarchy is part of our history, but we as a nation cannot live in the past. Our future as a nation is important, and by that I mean we must always protect our rights and freedoms. Of course we have symbols like our national anthem and our flag, but as a nation, as far as the oath of allegiance is concerned, I think its stands to reason and I think the majority of Canadians will agree, that people should swear allegiance to Canada and the Constitution.
Madam Speaker, enough said. I would be surprised if anyone could make a case against a proposal that is entirely in line with the changes that have been taken place in this country and with changing role in the world.
I think that if all Canadians had a chance to express their views here in this House, if they had that privilege, we would realize that, basically, our allegiance is to our country, Canada, and to the Constitution of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Vankoughnet (Hastings - Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must put on record my strong opposition to the amendment to the oath of citizenship within the Citizenship Act proposed in Bill C-285.
This bill seeks to erase a vital part of our heritage by removing reference to Her Majesty, the Queen's name, from Canada's oath of citizenship. The Crown is part and parcel of our Canadian heritage. It remains central to our constitutional monarchy. Every new Canadian learns this while going through the process of acquiring Canadian citizenship. Every person bom in Canada leams it through the education system.
By affirming the oath of citizenship new Canadians participate in a formal ceremony that is rooted in tradition. The oath of allegiance to the monarch has been part of the Canadian naturalization and citizenship process since 1868. Thus we have had oaths swearing allegiance to the Crown in Canada for more than 125 years.
It is absolutely clear that allegiance be sworn to the Queen of Canada. Canada is a constitutional monarchy. It is absurd to remove reference to the Crown from Canada's oath of citizenship when an oath of loyalty to the sovereign in accordance with the requirements of the Constitution Act of 1867 is sworn by members of Parliament before taking a seat in the House of Commons.
Our Constitution spells out very clearly that the Queen embodies a democratic system of Canadian government encompassing the House of Commons, the Senate, the Governor General and the Lieutenant Governors.
As a proud United Empire Loyalist descendant and a life member of the Monarchist League of Canada I know this country has a long tradition of continuous association with the institution of the monarchy.
The Queen is not a foreign monarch. She is a shared monarch recognized in some 50 countries either as sovereign or as head of the Commonwealth. In Canada she is Queen of Canada, represented in Canada by our Governor General.
Through our shared monarch we are linked with an incredibly diverse world-wide group of countries that produce many of our newest Canadians. For example, some of the Queen's most loyal subjects come from the West Indies and Hong Kong.
The Queen's lineage is only marginally British. She is a direct descendant of Louis IX of France and is related to most of the royal houses of Europe and others as diverse as the family of the Prophet and Genghis Khan.
As the Queen herself said at an official dinner in 1973:
It is as Queen of Canada that I am here, Queen of Canada and all Canadians, not just one or two ancestral strains. I want the Crown to be seen as a symbol of national sovereignty belonging to all.
May 27, 1993

It is not only a link between Commonwealth countries, but between Canadian citizens of every national origin or ancestry.
Over one-quarter of the world's countries are monarchies, including modern nations like Sweden and Japan. Independent monarchies and Commonwealth countries total about half the membership in the United Nations.
The monarchy is part of Canada's heritage, laid down by our Fathers of Confederation and most eloquently expressed by our first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1867 to his Queen with these words:
We have desired in this measure to declare in the most solemn and
emphatic manner our resolve to be under the sovereignty of Your
Majesty and your family forever.
As Canadians, we have embraced the Crown as a symbol of a strong Canadian parliamentary system and a strong democracy. The oath of citizenship is certainly part of that system.
This piece of legislation undermines the role and position of the monarchy in our government and Constitution and seeks to move Canada to an American styled government through a back door approach. It is thanks to the monarchy that unlike the United States or many other countries Canada has not had to endure a civil war.
For over 200 years the monarchy has been the most important influence in keeping our country together and creating a truly distinct society in North America.
The Crown has permitted and encouraged the development of representative institutions to serve Canadians whose ancestors have come from all corners of the world and has acted as a court of last appeal for all.
To remove reference to Her Majesty from the oath of citizenship represents an erosion of Canada's proud tradition of constitutional monarchy. Regretfully the New Democratic Party government in Ontario has removed reference from its oath for police officers.
Our Queen unites Canadians of every ethnic background and to remove reference to her in the oath of citizenship is simply not acceptable to myself nor my constituents in Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington.
Private Members' Business
Again, I oppose Bill C-285 to change the current oath of citizenship. I would like to take this opportunity to urge members of this House from all sides, especially those in the Liberal Party, to oppose this bill.

Madam Speaker, thank you for permitting me to participate in the debate on the private members' bill, Bill C-285, to amend the Citizenship Act proposed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.
Under the present oath of allegiance applicants for citizenship swear or affirm their allegiance to Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, her heirs and successors.
The bill before the House would remove reference to the monarchy in the oath of citizenship. This amendment addresses the symbolic aspect of the Citizenship Act rather than the broader issues of the act itself. As such it should be seen as a half measure.
Changes to the oath of citizenship, if any, must be done within the context of changes to the Citizenship Act. In that manner there will be broad and considered discussions among Canadians.
The oath of citizenship reflects the commitment of Canadians to uphold their citizenship and work for a better society. Acceptance of Canadian citizenship signified by the oath of citizenship also acknowledges that Canada has a strong history and heritage.
Part of that commitment to the family we call Canada is an acceptance of our multicultural background including the constitutional monarchy. Changing the oath of citizenship might be construed as a denial of an important aspect of Canadian ancestry. The oath as it stands strengthens the practical and symbolic elements of Canadian citizenship.
The wording of the oath of citizenship reflects our constitutional monarchy and acknowledges our national heritage, lb be a Canadian citizen is to accept and recognize that legacy. This amendment would jettison that legacy.
For new Canadians, taking the oath of citizenship is affirmation that they are accepted as equals and with the full rights and responsibilities that come with citizenship. For those reaffirming their citizenship it is confirmation that they are citizens of a nation that cherishes its

Adjournment Debate
heritage and yet builds for its future through the process of accepting people from around the world as Canadians.
The oath is affirmation or reaffirmation that all the rights and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship are understood and accepted by all citizens. It is apparent from the participation and citizenship ceremonies in 1992 that large numbers of people have no difficulty with the current oath of citizenship.
The number of citizenship applications in 1992-93, about 182,000, represents a 72 per cent increase since 1988. If the current oath of citizenship is causing new Canadians difficulty it is most unlikely that there would be the large increase in applications for Canadian citizenship. Similarly, if the current oath is a hindrance, it is doubtful that more than one million Canadians would have reaffirmed their citizenship as part of Canada 125 celebrations last year.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour for me to speak today on behalf of three million Canadian senior citizens. These are the people who made Canada what it is today.
On February 26 I questioned the Minister of State about the government's commitment to fund seniors
programs. Sadly the answer did not satisfy the senior citizens.
In 1988 the federal government made a commitment to spend $120 million over five years on seniors independence programs. Twenty million dollars was to be spent on research into Alzheimer's disease and osteoporosis under the Seniors Independence Research Program. As well, $100 million was to have been spent to help seniors with their daily living through the Seniors Independence Program. However, after the five years of these two programs, the government has spent little over half of what it has committed. What is the point of making a commitment if it is not going to live up to it?
On April 1 the minister announced $149 million over five years would be spent on three seniors programs: the Seniors Independence Research Program, the Seniors Independence Program and the Ventures in Independence Program. Once again the Canadian senior citizens and I question where the government's commitment is.
In the budget presented on April 26, the finance minister announced that the departmental grants and contributions are to be cut by 15 per cent in the coming years. The government's commitment to seniors independence lasted intact for a total of 25 days. If we divide $149 million over five years we get about $30 million a year. In the supplementary estimates given Thesday, the government plans on spending less than $19 million this year. Even before the budget cuts can take place, the government is already spending less than two-thirds of what it promised.
The government has tried to pass these cuts off as an attempt to reduce the deficit and the cost of government. The minister fails to realize that a little money spent now on independence programs will go a lot further in reducing the cost of government down the road. Instead of cutting $2 million for the Seniors Independence Research Program, the government should invest that money into finding a cure for Alzheimer's disease. Such a move would help hundreds of thousands of Canadians and save millions of dollars down the road.
The government's priorities are wrong. When will the minister realize that the government has not lived up to its commitment to seniors? When is the government going to realize that a little bit of money spent now makes a tremendous difference in the quality of life for millions of Canadian seniors? The seniors want to know why the government in 1988 would announce $120
May 27, 1993

million for these programs and then just spend a little over half of it.
In 1993 another announcement was made by the minister stating she was going to spend $149 million and as I indicated, it only stayed intact for 25 days. The senior citizens want to know why the government will not stand up to its commitments.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for putting this question tonight.
I would like to emphasize that the government really first demonstrated leadership in 1988 on this specific issue when we announced the five-year seniors strategy in strengthening the independence and quality of life of older Canadians.
Over the last five years substantial progress has been made. Community based contribution funding programs such as New Horizons and the Seniors Independence Program promote the independence of seniors and foster their involvement in self-help activities and partnerships that really create a good community resource.
Seniors are interested in having opportunities to contribute to their communities. Federally funded seniors projects mobilize thousands of these men and women who volunteer their time, their skills and their energy to health, education and cultural projects that deal with the quality of life of all Canadians.
To date the seniors strategy has supported more than 8,500 New Horizons programs and we project the involvement of 250,000 seniors each year and at least 500 seniors in the independence programs to date.
The Main Estimates, as my colleagues have mentioned, help both the current and future health and welfare social programs. In the 1993-94 edition, levels of funding for the seniors strategy may appear to be low due to the fact that they only represent original A-base of New Horizons and the National Advisory Council on Aging along with a small reprofiled sum for the Seniors Independence Program. But those figures do not imply that expenditure reductions have been made to the seniors strategy.
Adjournment Debate
As you are aware, Madam Speaker, all the elements of the strategies were due to sunset on March 31, 1993. So on April 1 the Minister of State for Seniors announced that the federal government will provide $170 million over the next five years to continue seniors strategy programs. In particular, a total of $149 million will be available to support community programs for the seniors combined with funds already allocated to the New Horizons and the National Advisory Council on Aging for a total of $234 million. That is available through this strategy to enhance the independence and the quality of life for seniors.
I also have to say that the seniors do form a very important part of our society. We recognize this more and more each day. One thing we have done is we have lowered interest rates, we have lowered inflation and the main thing of that is the dollar today will be worth a dollar tomorrow.
All of us here in this House and all of us across Canada will have to contribute to deficit debt reduction.

Madam Speaker, Chuck Davis, in his column in the Vancouver Daily Province of Sunday, February 21 of this year reports that Roderick Haig-Brown, a B.C. judge, writer, fishermen and naturalist, would have been 85 on that day.
Mr. Haig-Brown once wrote: "If weakness and indecision allow the salmon in their abundance to disappear from the rivers and the ocean what hope can there be for the future of life itself".
It is a good time to ask that question of ourselves with respect to the salmon on the west coast of British Columbia. The year 1992 should have been a very good year for the Stuart Lake run. It is a run that was almost wiped out some years ago and the commercial fishermen have not been fishing this particular run in the low cycle year hoping to rebuild it. This was the year when their efforts were going to bear fruit. Two hundred thousand sockeye should have reached Stuart Lake.
The Department of Fisheries knows that the sockeye have passed the mission gates. They were on the way up, but when it came to arriving at Stuart Lake there were something like 47,000, just 23 per cent of the expectation. It was a disaster. The minister of fisheries said it

Adjournment Debate
was a great success story because 47,000 was more than ever before in the low cycle year.
We were hoping and expecting and knew there were 200,000 in the river. DFO early on said that 1.2 million sockeye had gone missing from the river after going through the Mission gates. The Pearse-Larkin report identified a figure in the neighbourhood of 500,000.
Whichever figure is right does not matter. It is still a tremendous number of sockeye to go missing and there is little doubt about what happened. They were fished, no question about that. It was no coincidence. No one would believe it was just a coincidence that this was the first year of the aboriginal fisheries strategy being introduced.
The minister recognized there was a problem and commissioned the Pearse-Larkin report. He got a lot of information and said that in 1993 there would be no aboriginal fisheries strategy unless a watershed agreement was reached with all of the bands along the Fraser River.
He reported recently that he has a watershed agreement with respect to the Skeena. A couple of weeks ago he said he had one with respect to the Fraser for almost all of the bands. More recently it has been made public that the agreement is only with some 50 per cent of the bands along the Fraser River. However, he is proceeding with the aboriginal fisheries strategy in the Fraser River this year as well.
The Sto:Lo Nation said it is not going to pay attention to the new scheme for the aboriginal fisheries strategy. It told DFO some weeks in advance that it intended to fish twice as long as the recent opening for Chinook. That is a fish species which has not been fished because the numbers have been threatened. Therefore, the commercial fishermen have been leaving them.
This year the natives were given one day for food fishery at that particular time. Instead of that they said weeks in advance that they were going to take two days. DFO apparently did nothing. It was informed in writing yet did nothing until the day the boats actually appeared on the scene and were fishing when the minister's officials went in and seized the nets.
However, the officials did not charge anybody, nobody at all. The minister said the reason they did not charge them was that the native fishermen who were fishing did not know they were breaking the regulations.
Somebody knew but nobody was charged. The minister in effect is saying to these people: "Go ahead and break all the regulations you want, any time you want, anywhere you want. Damage the species as much as you want. Threaten the resources as much as you want. We will find some way of not charging anybody so that we are not going to be embarrassed by taking these cases to court".
It was a disastrous year last year. This year is shaping up to be another disastrous year for the salmon on the B.C. west coast.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague from British Columbia for bringing forward this most essential issue of the missing sockeye, especially in the area of the Stuart Lake region.
We do need the valuable fishing industry in British Columbia and it can only be accomplished by enhancing the co-operative attitude by all the parties that are involved.
The government developed the aboriginal fisheries strategy to resolve the uncertainty left by the Sparrow decision of 1990 which gave the aboriginal people the right to fish for food in social and ceremonial purposes. The aboriginal fisheries strategy initiated a multi-year approach to satisfying aboriginal communities' aspirations for greater involvement in fisheries management and harvesting within the context of maintaining a healthy resource.
This summer the fishery will run more smoothly than last summer when there were many difficulties. The process of implementing aboriginal agreements under the fisheries strategy is going to be faster and it is going to be quicker.
In achieving the objectives of having watershed agreements the B.C. First Nations and DFO have begun the process of bringing the Fraser watershed groups together. Those First Nations have signed a memorandum of understanding indicating their willingness to work together to arrive at a watershed-wide agreement with DFO regarding a co-ordinated approach.
May 27, 1993

In fact those First Nations of the lower and upper Fraser have already signed the Fraser watershed agreement. The First Nations of the middle Fraser are expected to sign on to that agreement in the near future.
In conclusion I want to tell the member that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans intends to press forward with the aboriginal fisheries strategy in 1993 because we know negotiations are better than litigation
Adjournment Debate
and we still have to work within the Supreme Court decision.
